assets.topic: Ariely's Origin Story: The Burn Ward and the Birth of a Research Agenda
assets.visual_frame_description: Split scene: Left side — an 18-year-old in burn bandages, being treated by nurses who rip bandages off quickly. Right side — the same person years later, as a professor conducting experiments. Arrows show the connection: his personal pain experience led to systematic research on pain perception, which led to the broader field of behavioral economics.
assets.target_channel: Personal Motivation | Scientific Discovery | Pain Perception
assets.question: How did Ariely's personal experience with severe burns and the bandage-removal process shape his research agenda and lead to the field of behavioral economics?
assets.correct_cue: Ariely's third-degree burns (covering 70% of his body) gave him years of direct experience with medical pain. He noticed that nurses ripped bandages off quickly (causing intense short bursts) because they believed this minimized total pain. But Ariely's own experience suggested slower, gentler removal was less agonizing overall, even though it took longer. His subsequent experiments showed that the duration and pattern of pain matter — people preferred longer, lower-intensity pain over shorter, higher-intensity pain. This mismatch between what caregivers believed and what patients actually experienced revealed a fundamental insight: people's intuitive theories about their own and others' behavior are often wrong, and only systematic experimentation can reveal the truth. This insight became the foundation of his work in behavioral economics — the study of how people actually make decisions (often irrationally) versus how standard economic theory says they should.
distractors: Ariely's research focus came from his academic training in economics — he noticed that classic economic models didn't match real-world data
Ariely became interested in irrationality after watching other patients make bad medical decisions that contradicted their own stated preferences
Ariely's burn injury made him want to help other burn victims, so he designed experiments to test bandage removal techniques
assets.underlying_psychology: Ariely's personal experience illustrates a core theme of behavioral economics: the gap between intuitive theories and empirical reality. The nurses were experienced, well-meaning, and confident in their approach — yet they were systematically wrong. This is because humans are prone to 'theory-induced blindness': once we have a theory (quick removal = less total pain), we stop testing it against experience. Behavioral economics emerged from recognizing that these systematic errors are not random but predictable — hence the book's title.
assets.player_mission: How did Ariely's personal experience with severe burns and the bandage-removal process shape his research agenda and lead to the field of behavioral economics?

assets.topic: The Decoy Effect: How a Useless Third Option Changes Your Choice
assets.subject_baseline: The Economist magazine offered three subscription options: (A) Internet-only for $59, (B) Print-only for $125, (C) Print-and-Internet for $125. When all three were presented, 84% of MIT students chose option C and 16% chose A — zero chose B. But when option B (the 'decoy') was removed, only 32% chose C and 68% chose A. The mere presence of an option that NO ONE selected completely flipped the preferences.
assets.interrogation_transcript: Researcher: 'Why did you choose the print-and-Internet combo?' Participant: 'Because it's clearly the best deal. You get both for the same price as print alone.' Researcher: 'But what if the print-only option had never existed?' Participant: 'I'd probably just get the Internet. That's all I really need.' Researcher: 'So adding an option you'd never choose changed your mind?' Participant: 'I... I guess so. But it doesn't feel that way.'
observed_nonverbal_log: The decoy option (print-only at $125) was selected by 0% of participants, yet it profoundly shaped choices
Removing the decoy caused a 36-point swing toward the cheaper option
Participants denied being influenced by the decoy when asked
The decoy works by creating an easy relative comparison: C is clearly better than B, so C looks better overall
The same effect operates in real-world pricing: high-priced menu items make the second-most-expensive look reasonable
assets.question: How does the 'decoy effect' exploit our reliance on relative comparisons, and why does adding an inferior option make a different option seem more attractive?
assets.correct_diagnosis: The decoy effect works because humans lack an internal value meter — we don't know the absolute worth of things. Instead, we judge value by comparing options against each other. A decoy option that is clearly worse than one of the alternatives (but not obviously worse than the other) creates a 'relative comparison advantage' for that alternative. In the Economist case, the print-only option ($125) was clearly worse than the combo ($125 for both), making the combo look like a steal. In the real estate case, a colonial house needing a new roof makes the identical colonial without roof problems seem obviously superior. The decoy doesn't need to be chosen — it just needs to be present to anchor a comparison.
distractors: The decoy effect only works with subscription services — it doesn't apply to physical products or major life decisions
People who are given time to think rationally are immune to the decoy effect
The decoy works because consumers assume the company has priced items rationally, so they infer the combo must be the best value
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Stage 1 — Relativity instinct: Humans are wired to compare. We can't help evaluating things relative to each other. Stage 2 — Comparison difficulty: When options differ on multiple attributes, direct comparison is hard. Stage 3 — Decoy insertion: Adding an option that is similar to but worse than one alternative creates a simple comparative frame. Stage 4 — Asymmetric dominance: The target option now dominates the decoy on all dimensions, making it seem superior overall. Stage 5 — Choice shift: The target's enhanced apparent value shifts choices away from competing options.

assets.topic: The Menu Pricing Dilemma: Engineering Choices with Decoys
assets.scenario_setup: You own a restaurant. Your food consultant (Greg Rapp) tells you that you're losing money because your pricing strategy doesn't account for relativity. Currently, your most expensive entrée is $28; your mid-range options cluster around $18-$22. 'Add a $45 lobster dish,' he says. 'Nobody will buy it, but it will boost your profits.'
assets.initial_dialogue: Chef: 'That's insane. Why would we put a $45 dish on the menu that no one will order? It'll just sit there. And what if someone actually orders it? We don't even have lobster.' You: 'The consultant says it will make the $26 filet mignon look reasonable by comparison.' Chef: 'So we're using psychology to trick people into spending more? That feels dishonest.'

choices.text: 'It's not dishonest — it's giving people context. Humans naturally evaluate options relative to each other. The $45 dish provides an anchor that helps customers recognize the value of the $26 filet. As long as the filet is fairly priced and high quality, we're helping customers make a decision they'll be happy with. The consultant's data shows that restaurants with a high-priced decoy have higher average check sizes AND higher customer satisfaction — people feel good about getting a 'deal' on the second-most-expensive option.'
choices.feedback: This is Ariely's point: relativity is an inescapable feature of human cognition. Using it is not manipulation — it's recognizing how people actually make decisions. The $45 dish provides a reference point that makes the $26 dish feel like a good value. Customers who choose it feel smart, not tricked.

choices.text: 'You're right, it's manipulation. We should price everything fairly relative to cost, with a modest markup. Let customers evaluate the food on its merits, not on how it compares to an artificially inflated option.'
choices.feedback: This is ethically clean but ignores how people actually make decisions. Even without a decoy, customers will compare your $28 dish to competitors' prices, to what they remember paying elsewhere, or to their internal sense of what a meal 'should' cost. Relativity is inescapable.

choices.text: 'Let's add the $45 dish but make it a real, high-quality option — a special lobster preparation that costs us $25 to make. If someone orders it, great — we make a profit. If not, it serves as an anchor. Win-win.'
choices.feedback: This tries to have it both ways. But now you have inventory risk (lobster that spoils) and the dish might actually sell at a lower margin than the filet. The power of the decoy is precisely that it doesn't need to sell — its job is to be a reference point.

assets.theoretical_principle: The decoy effect (also called 'asymmetric dominance') is one of the most robust findings in behavioral economics. It shows that preferences are not pre-existing and stable — they are constructed at the moment of choice based on the available context. Adding an option that is clearly worse than one alternative (but not the other) shifts choices toward that alternative. This is the 'attraction effect' — the decoy 'attracts' attention to the target by making it look dominant.

assets.topic: Arbitrary Coherence: How Random Anchors Shape Our Willingness to Pay
assets.question: Ariely's social security number experiment showed that students with high-ending digits (80-99) bid 216-346% more for the same products than students with low-ending digits (1-20). How does this demonstrate 'arbitrary coherence' in pricing?
assets.correct_answer: Arbitrary coherence describes two linked phenomena: (1) 'Arbitrary' — initial prices (anchors) can be influenced by completely irrelevant factors, like the last two digits of your social security number. (2) 'Coherence' — once that anchor is set, it shapes all subsequent price judgments in a logically consistent way. Students didn't just anchor on their SS digits for one product — the anchor carried across related products. If they anchored high on the Côtes du Rhône wine, they also anchored high on the Hermitage wine (a related product). The anchor creates a 'coherent' price landscape where relative values remain sensible even though absolute values are arbitrary.
distractors: The social security number effect was a fluke — it only appeared in one experiment and has never been replicated
People are consciously aware of anchoring effects and can correct for them if they try harder
Anchoring only affects people who are uncertain about the product category — experts are immune
assets.explanation: Ariely's anchoring experiment is a cornerstone of behavioral economics. It shows that the first price we encounter for a product imprints on us like goslings imprinting on their mother (Lorenz's studies). This 'imprint' becomes an anchor that shapes all future price judgments in that category. The arbitrariness is the disturbing part: the anchor could be your SS number, the MSRP, or even the current temperature. But the coherence is the adaptive part: once anchored, relative pricing within a category remains rational. This explains how different people can have vastly different willingness-to-pay for the same product — they were anchored on different initial prices.

Once the first decision is made, later decisions follow in what seems a logical and coherent manner - the die is cast and the anchor set

Our sensitivity to price changes might be largely a result of our memory for past prices and our desire for coherence with past decisions

assets.topic: The Pearl King: How Salvador Assael Created a Market for Black Pearls
assets.visual_frame_description: A split visual: Left side — a pile of gunmetal-gray Tahitian black pearls, unattractive and unsold. Right side — the same pearls displayed in Harry Winston's Fifth Avenue window, nestled among diamonds and rubies, with an outrageously high price tag. Arrows show: 'Same pearls. Different anchor. Different perceived value.'
assets.question: How did Salvador Assael create a market for Tahitian black pearls, and what does this reveal about the relationship between price and perceived value?
assets.correct_cue: Assael initially failed to sell the pearls at low prices — they were gunmetal gray and looked like musket balls. Then he took the best specimens to Harry Winston, who displayed them with a high price tag among diamonds and rubies in his Fifth Avenue window, while Assael ran ads showing them alongside gems. The high price ANCHORED the pearls as luxury items. Once that anchor was set, the pearls' perceived value was established. The pearls hadn't changed — only the context in which they were presented. This illustrates that value is not intrinsic; it is constructed from contextual cues, especially the first price we encounter (the anchor).
distractors: The black pearls eventually sold because their quality improved over time as better specimens were harvested
Assael's success was due to a celebrity endorsement — a famous actress wore them and created demand
The black pearl market was an accident — Assael tried to sell them cheap but nobody wanted them, so he raised the price out of desperation
assets.underlying_psychology: The black pearl story is Ariely's favorite example of how 'supply and demand' is not a law of nature but a psychological phenomenon. In standard economics, price is determined by supply and demand. But the pearl king reversed this: he set a high price first, and that price created the demand. The high price signaled exclusivity, quality, and desirability. Once consumers accepted the anchor, they made 'coherent' subsequent judgments about the pearls' value. This is the 'Veblen effect' — higher price increases demand because price itself is a signal of value.

assets.topic: BOSS BATTLE: The Power of FREE! — When Zero Is Not Just Another Number
assets.stage_1_observation: Ariely's chocolate experiment: Lindt truffles (30¢ each) vs. Hershey's Kisses. Condition 1: Truffle 15¢, Kiss 1¢ → 73% chose truffle, 27% chose Kiss. Condition 2: Truffle 14¢, Kiss FREE → 31% chose truffle, 69% chose Kiss. Both prices dropped by 1¢, relative difference unchanged — yet behavior flipped completely. The same effect replicated when truffle was 25¢/Kiss free, 26¢/1¢, etc.
assets.stage_1_question: Why does reducing the price of both options by the same amount (preserving relative difference) cause a complete reversal of preference when one option becomes free?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Zero is not just another number. Most transactions involve weighing upside vs. downside risk. But when something is FREE, there is no perceived downside — no risk of making a bad decision. The fear of loss (one of the most powerful human motivators) is eliminated entirely. So the emotional appeal of FREE overrides the rational cost-benefit calculation that would normally lead us to choose the better product. In the chocolate experiment, the Lindt truffle was objectively the better deal at both price points, but FREE! short-circuited the comparison process. This is the 'zero price effect' — demand for a free item is disproportionately higher than would be predicted by standard economic models.
assets.stage_2_intervention: You are a policy advisor designing a public health campaign to reduce soda consumption. Two approaches: (A) Tax sugary drinks — a 20¢ surcharge on each can, making them more expensive relative to healthier options. (B) Subsidize healthy drinks — make sparkling water FREE at public fountains and school cafeterias.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Approach B is likely more effective because of the zero price effect. Making healthy options FREE triggers the emotional appeal of zero — people will overwhelmingly choose free options even if the taxed soda is 'only' slightly more expensive. The asymmetry is: a 20¢ surcharge on soda (loss frame) will cause some reduction, but making water FREE (zero frame) will cause a disproportionately larger shift. Behavioral economics predicts that free healthy options will have a larger impact on behavior than equivalent taxes on unhealthy ones, because FREE bypasses rational cost-benefit calculation and triggers an emotional hot button.
assets.boss_battle_explanation: Ariely identifies FREE! as an 'emotional hot button' — it triggers an irrational surge of excitement that overrides normal decision-making. The evolutionary logic: in ancestral environments, free resources (water, fruit, shelter) were genuinely valuable and worth grabbing without deliberation. This heuristic served us well for most of human history. But in modern consumer environments, FREE! is often a trap — it leads us to take things we don't need, wait in lines that aren't worth it, and accept inferior products. The boss battle is learning to recognize when FREE is a genuine opportunity versus when it's a manipulation that leads us away from what we actually want.

assets.topic: When Money Ruins Thanksgiving: The Collision of Social and Market Norms
assets.subject_baseline: You are at your mother-in-law's Thanksgiving dinner. The turkey is perfect, the company warm. You pull out your wallet and ask, 'Mom, for all this love and effort, how much do I owe you?' Silence. Red faces. Tears. Next year's invitation never comes.
assets.interrogation_transcript: Researcher: 'Why would offering money for Thanksgiving dinner be offensive?' Anthropologist: 'Because it's a violation of social norms — the unwritten rules of gift-giving, hospitality, and family obligation.' Behavioral economist: 'But why does a simple payment cause such outrage? Because we live in TWO worlds: the SOCIAL world (favors, gifts, community — warm and fuzzy) and the MARKET world (wages, prices, payments — sharp-edged and transactional). Offering money for Thanksgiving rips the relationship out of the social world and drops it into the market world. Once that happens, the relationship is fundamentally changed.'
observed_nonverbal_log: The exact same task (dragging circles across a screen) produced different effort levels depending on framing: paid $5 → 159 circles; paid 50¢ → 101 circles; unpaid social favor → 168 circles
Lawyers offered $30/hr to help needy retirees said no; asked to do it for FREE, they said yes
Small gifts (Snickers bar, Godiva chocolates) kept people in social norm mode and produced high effort
Mentioning the monetary value of a gift ('a 50-cent Snickers bar') switched people back to market norms and reduced effort
Just THINKING about money (scrambled-sentence task with salary-related words) made people more self-reliant, less helpful, and less social
assets.question: What distinguishes social norms from market norms, and why does introducing money into a social relationship change the nature of the exchange?
assets.correct_diagnosis: Social norms are governed by friendship, community, and reciprocity — payment is not expected immediately, favors are given freely, and the relationship is warm. Market norms are governed by prices, wages, and cost-benefit calculations — you get what you pay for, and the relationship is transactional. The two systems are mutually exclusive: activating market norms (by mentioning money, price, or salary) pushes out social norms and vice versa. Once a relationship has been recast as a market exchange, it is very difficult to return to social norms. The monetary amount doesn't matter — even a small payment for a favor switches the frame. The key insight: small gifts maintain social norms, but mentioning the cost of the gift converts it to a market transaction.
distractors: Social and market norms are compatible — you can pay friends for favors and maintain the same warm relationship
People work harder for money than for free because money is a stronger motivator than social obligation
Social norms are primitive and disappear in modern societies where most exchanges are monetary
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Stage 1 — Dual worlds: Humans evolved both social reciprocity systems (favors, gifts, sharing) and market exchange systems (barter, trade, payment). Stage 2 — Mutual exclusivity: These systems are managed by different neural circuits and cannot operate simultaneously. Stage 3 — Frame collision: Introducing market elements (money, price, cost) into a social relationship activates the market frame, suppressing the social frame. Stage 4 — Relationship damage: Once the market frame is activated, the relationship is perceived as transactional. Trust, warmth, and generosity decline. Stage 5 — Asymmetric recovery: Returning from market to social norms is very difficult — the monetary frame sticks.
assets.player_mission: What distinguishes social norms from market norms, and why does introducing money into a social relationship change the nature of the exchange?
assets.visual_frame_description: A double-column ledger book: warm entries fill the social side, sharp entries the market side, and any item that crosses the middle leaves a scorch mark.
key_concepts: We live simultaneously in two worlds: social norms (friendly requests, warm, no instant payback required) and market norms (wages, prices, rents, comparable benefits, prompt payment)

assets.topic: The Halloween Cookie Experiment: Gifts vs. Payments
assets.scenario_setup: You are a manager trying to motivate your team. You have two options for a bonus: (A) A cash bonus of $50. (B) A gift — a nice bottle of wine worth about $50. Your HR director says option B is 'wasteful and inefficient — why not just give them the cash so they can buy what they actually want?' But you remember Ariely's finding about gifts vs. payments.
assets.initial_dialogue: HR Director: 'I ran the numbers. A $50 cash bonus costs us exactly $50. A $50 bottle of wine costs us $50 wholesale but the employee values it at maybe $35 retail. Cash is more efficient — it's worth more to the employee and costs us the same. Gifts are economically irrational.' You remember Ariely's experiment: kids who got 3 Hershey's Kisses as a gift were happy to trade 1 Kiss for a small Snickers or 2 Kisses for a large Snickers. But when you call it a 'sale' instead of a 'gift,' the exchange frame changes behavior completely.

choices.text: 'You're right about the economics, but wrong about the psychology. The wine stays in the SOCIAL norm frame — it feels like a gift, a gesture of appreciation. Cash triggers MARKET norms — the employee evaluates it against their salary, decides if it's 'enough,' and starts thinking transactionally. A gift worth $35 to the employee might motivate more than $50 cash, because the gift signals appreciation (social) while cash signals payment (market). The bottle of wine says 'I thought about you.' assets.theoretical_principle: Ariely's Halloween experiment revealed that the frame (gift vs. payment) fundamentally changes behavior. When the same interaction was framed as a 'sale' (you have 3 Kisses, you can buy a Snickers for 1 or 2 Kisses), kids became less willing to trade. The 'gift' frame activates social norms (generosity, reciprocity); the 'sale' frame activates market norms (self-interest, getting a good deal). Gifts maintain relationships; prices destroy them.

assets.topic: BOSS BATTLE: The Hot-Cold Empathy Gap — You Don't Know Your Aroused Self
assets.stage_1_observation: Ariely's Berkeley experiment: male students answered questions about sexual preferences, morality, and safe sex in two states. In a 'cold' state (not aroused): they predicted they would never engage in risky or immoral sexual behavior. In a 'hot' state (sexually aroused via masturbation while viewing erotic images): their predicted willingness to engage in the same behaviors nearly DOUBLED. The same people. The same questions. Different answers.
assets.stage_1_question: Why can't people in a 'cold' emotional state accurately predict their own preferences and behaviors when they will be in a 'hot' emotional state?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The 'hot-cold empathy gap' (Loewenstein, 1996) describes our inability to accurately predict how we will feel and behave when we are in a different emotional state. When we are 'cold' (calm, rational), we underestimate the power of visceral drives — hunger, thirst, anger, fear, sexual arousal. We think 'I would never do that' because we are judging our future behavior from an emotional state that lacks the visceral component. But when the visceral state hits, it rewrites our priorities, amplifies certain desires, and suppresses long-term considerations. The key finding: this gap is not just about poor prediction — it's about a fundamental inability to simulate a different emotional state. As Ariely puts it: 'We are all Homer Simpson in the box of doughnuts — we know we shouldn't, but when the doughnuts are in front of us...'
assets.stage_2_intervention: You are designing a sex education program for teenagers. One approach: show graphic images of STDs and pregnancy risks to scare them into safe behavior (traditional scare tactics). Another approach: have them role-play situations where peer pressure and arousal might override their intentions, and practice precommitting to safe behaviors before they are in a 'hot' state.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: The second approach is more effective. Scare tactics assume teenagers are rational calculators who weigh risks in the moment — but the hot-cold empathy gap means that in a 'hot' (aroused, peer-pressured) state, abstract risks lose their power. Precommitment strategies — making decisions about condom use BEFORE the arousing situation, rehearsing refusal scripts, carrying condoms at all times — work WITH the empathy gap rather than against it. The key is to help teenagers recognize that their 'cold' self cannot fully control their 'hot' self, and build structural safeguards accordingly.
assets.boss_battle_explanation: The hot-cold empathy gap is one of the most important and underappreciated findings in behavioral science. It explains why we repeatedly fail to act on our own best intentions: we make commitments in a 'cool' state (diets, budgets, fidelity) that our 'hot' selves cannot keep. The gap affects not just sexual behavior but also hunger (we shop when hungry and buy more), anger (we promise not to lose our temper), and every other visceral state. The solution is not willpower — it's precommitment and environmental design that protects our future 'hot' selves from our present 'cold' overconfidence.

assets.topic: Deadlines as Commitment Devices: Fighting Procrastination with Precommitment
assets.visual_frame_description: A timeline of a 12-week semester showing three classes. Class A (top): No deadlines except final — grades worst. Class B (middle): Self-imposed deadlines with penalties — grades middle. Class C (bottom): Externally imposed equally-spaced deadlines — grades best. The visual shows that freedom without structure = worst outcomes, and externally forced pacing = best outcomes.
assets.question: What did Ariely's experiment with three differently-structured deadline policies reveal about procrastination and the effectiveness of commitment devices?
assets.correct_cue: Ariely gave three classes the same three-paper assignment. Class 1 had no deadlines (just a final due date) — they got the worst grades, procrastinated most, and had the most late penalties. Class 2 had self-imposed deadline choices (set their own spaced deadlines with late penalties) — got middle grades. Class 3 had externally imposed equally-spaced deadlines — got the best grades. The results show: (1) People DO procrastinate without external structure. (2) Many people recognize their procrastination and will use commitment devices (self-imposed deadlines) to fight it — and this helps. (3) But self-imposed deadlines are imperfect — some people don't space them enough. (4) External structure is most effective because it forces optimal pacing. The implication: we need tools that help our rational 'planning' selves constrain our impulsive 'doing' selves.
distractors: The no-deadline class did best because they had the most flexibility and could work at their own pace
Self-imposed deadlines were equally effective as externally imposed ones — the key is having any deadline at all
Procrastination is a character flaw that can be overcome with willpower and better time management
assets.underlying_psychology: Ariely's deadline experiment demonstrates the two-self model of self-control. We have a 'planner' self (who wants to save, diet, and work steadily) and a 'doer' self (who wants to spend, eat, and procrastinate). Commitment devices — tools that bind our future selves — help the planner constrain the doer. The most effective commitment devices are externally enforced (automatic savings deductions, fixed deadlines). Self-imposed commitments help but are weaker because the doer can override them. This is why Ulysses had himself tied to the mast — he knew his future self would be weak.

assets.topic: The Savings Crisis: Why We Can't Save and What Precommitment Can Do
assets.question: Why do Americans save less than 1% of their income (negative savings rate in 2006) while Europeans save 20%, Japanese 25%, and Chinese 50%? And what behavioral economic solutions address this?
assets.correct_answer: The proximate cause is a combination of rampant consumerism, easy credit (6 billion credit card solicitations in 2005 alone, average household credit card debt ~$9,000), and the human tendency toward immediate gratification. The deeper cause is the same hot-cold empathy gap: in a 'cold' state, we plan to save; in a 'hot' state (seeing something we want), we spend. The behavioral solution is precommitment: automatic savings plans (like 'Save More Tomorrow' — Thaler & Benartzi) that commit future salary increases to savings BEFORE we have a chance to spend them. By making savings automatic and removing the decision from the hot state, these programs dramatically increased savings rates. Standard economic theory says people will save when it's rational to do so; behavioral economics shows people need help binding their future selves.
distractors: Americans save less because they have lower incomes than Europeans or Japanese — savings rates are determined by income, not psychology
Credit card companies are to blame — if credit were less available, Americans would save more naturally
The solution is financial education — once people understand compound interest and the need for retirement savings, they will save more
assets.explanation: Ariely uses the American savings crisis to illustrate the gap between intention and action. We KNOW we should save. We INTEND to save. But in the moment of purchase, the immediate pleasure outweighs the abstract future benefit. Precommitment works by making the decision to save in a 'cold' state — and then locking it in before the 'hot' state arrives. 'Save More Tomorrow' programs increase savings from 3.5% to 13.6% of income over 40 months, simply by asking people to commit FUTURE raises (which they haven't yet experienced) to savings. This leverages loss aversion: we don't miss money we never had.

assets.topic: The Duke Basketball Ticket Experiment: Why Owners Value What They Have 14x More Than Buyers
assets.subject_baseline: Duke University basketball tickets are allocated through a lottery among students who camp out for days in 'Krzyzewskiville.' After the lottery, winners and losers have had identical camping experiences and are equally passionate fans. Yet winners (owners) demanded an average of $2,400 to sell their ticket, while losers (buyers) were willing to pay an average of $175. Not a SINGLE transaction was possible — no owner would sell at any price a buyer would pay.
assets.interrogation_transcript: Winner (Joseph): 'This game is a defining memory of my time at Duke. I'll tell my children and grandchildren about it. How can you put a price on that?' Loser (William): 'For $175 I can watch at a sports bar with friends, drink beer, eat food, and have money left over for CDs.' Researcher: 'You both camped for the same week. You both love Duke basketball. The only difference is the lottery.' Winner: 'But I HAVE the ticket now. It's mine. I can already imagine being there.'
observed_nonverbal_log: Winners and losers had IDENTICAL camping experiences and basketball passion before the lottery
Within minutes of the lottery, a 14x gap in valuation appeared
Buyers focused on ALTERNATIVE USES of money (sports bar, CDs, shoes)
Sellers focused on the EXPERIENCE THEY WOULD LOSE (memories, defining moments)
This is the endowment effect: ownership instantly increases perceived value
assets.question: What is the endowment effect, and what three psychological quirks does Ariely identify as its causes?
assets.correct_diagnosis: The endowment effect (Kahneman, Knetsch, Thaler) is the tendency to value something more once we own it — sellers demand more than buyers will pay. Ariely identifies three causes: (1) We fall in love with what we have — ownership creates emotional attachment almost instantly (the China adoption story: random baby assignments felt 'perfect' to each couple within hours). (2) We focus on what we might LOSE rather than what we might GAIN — loss aversion makes selling feel painful. (3) We assume others will see the same value we do — we project our own attachment onto potential buyers. These quirks explain why people hold onto stocks too long, demand more for their house than buyers will pay, and find it almost impossible to sell things they own.
distractors: The endowment effect only applies to sentimental items (basketball tickets, family heirlooms) — not to ordinary consumer goods
The 14x gap in the Duke experiment was because the winners were wealthier students who could afford to demand more
The endowment effect is rational — owners have better information about the item's true value than potential buyers
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Stage 1 — Instant attachment: Within moments of ownership, we begin to value the object more. The Chinese adoption story illustrates this: random baby assignments felt divinely guided within hours. Stage 2 — Loss frame: When selling, we focus on what we'll lose (the experience, the memories), not on what we'll gain (money for other things). Stage 3 — Projection: We assume buyers will share our valuation, so we're offended by low offers. Stage 4 — Market failure: The gap between seller and buyer valuations prevents efficient exchange. Both parties are worse off: the seller doesn't get cash, the buyer doesn't get the item.

assets.topic: The Door-Closing Problem: Why We Keep Too Many Options Open
assets.visual_frame_description: A person trying to walk through a hallway with 50 doors on each side. They try to keep every door open — running back and forth, holding doors with their feet, elbows, and chin. They're exhausted. They're going nowhere. The caption: 'When you try to keep every door open, you never get through any of them.'
assets.question: Ariely's experiment showed that when participants had to click on two doors (one that closed permanently, one that never closed) to earn money, they irrationally chased the shrinking door that was about to close — even when the other door offered higher rewards. Why do humans hate closing doors, and what cost does this incur?
assets.correct_cue: Humans have an irrational aversion to closing doors — we want to keep options open even when keeping them open is costly. This is because we anticipate regret: if we close a door permanently, we might later wish we hadn't. In Ariely's experiment, participants would chase the disappearing door rather than focus on the stable high-value door, earning significantly less money. The fear of lost opportunity (anticipated regret) outweighed the real opportunity available. In real life, this manifests as: holding unprofitable stocks rather than selling them, staying in bad relationships 'just in case,' keeping old clothes we never wear, and refusing to commit to a career path because another might be better. The cost is that keeping doors open consumes attention, energy, and time — and prevents us from fully committing to the paths we do choose.
distractors: Keeping options open is always rational — you never know when a backup plan might be needed
The door-closing aversion only applies to trivial decisions, not major life choices like careers or relationships
People who keep multiple options open are happier because they feel less trapped by their decisions
assets.underlying_psychology: This chapter challenges the common-sense idea that more options = better. Ariely argues that our irrational desire to keep doors open is connected to loss aversion and the endowment effect. We treat potential future options as if we already own them, and closing a door feels like a loss. But this 'hedonic flexibility' comes at a cost: spreading ourselves thin, never fully committing, and experiencing less satisfaction with what we do choose because we're always wondering about the road not taken. The solution: deliberately close doors to force commitment.

assets.topic: Coke vs. Pepsi: How Brand Expectations Override Taste
assets.question: In blind taste tests, Pepsi often beats Coke (more people prefer the sweeter taste). But in labeled tests, Coke wins overwhelmingly. What does this reveal about the power of expectations on our actual experience?
assets.correct_answer: When people know the brand, their EXPECTATIONS about Coke (based on years of marketing, brand associations, and cultural meaning) override the actual sensory experience. The brand expectation literally changes the neural processing of taste — fMRI shows that when people drink labeled Coke, the hippocampus and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (memory and meaning centers) activate more than when drinking unlabeled Coke. The expectation of 'Coke' creates a more positive experience than the unlabeled beverage. This is the 'placebo effect' applied to consumer goods: our expectations about an experience shape the experience itself. This doesn't make the preference for Coke 'unreal' — it means taste is not purely sensory but is constructed from sensory input PLUS expectation.
distractors: Coke actually tastes better than Pepsi — the blind test results were flawed because participants knew they were in a taste test
Brand preferences are purely cultural — people learn to prefer Coke because of advertising, and this has no effect on actual taste perception
The Coke vs. Pepsi difference is just about sugar content — no psychological or neural expectation effect is involved
assets.explanation: Ariely uses the Coke-Pepsi paradox to show that experience is not a direct readout of sensory data — it's a construction that combines sensory input with expectations. When we expect something to be good (because of a brand, a high price, or a prestigious venue), it LITERALLY tastes better to us, because the expectation changes neural processing. This is the basis of the placebo effect: believing a treatment will work makes it more likely to work. Expectations are not just about marketing — they shape our experience of movies, wine, food, relationships, and even pain.

assets.topic: The Movie Preview Problem: Do Spoilers Ruin the Experience?
assets.scenario_setup: Two friends are arguing about movie previews. Friend A avoids all trailers and reviews — 'spoilers ruin everything.' Friend B watches every trailer and reads reviews — 'I want to know what I'm getting into.' They ask you: who will enjoy the movie more?
assets.initial_dialogue: Friend A: 'If I know the plot twists, the movie is ruined. I want a pure, unspoiled experience.' Friend B: 'That's ridiculous. If I know it's good, I relax and enjoy it. I'm never disappointed because I know what to expect. Besides, studies show that spoiled stories are MORE enjoyable because you can appreciate how the story unfolds.'

A spoiler doesn't ruin enjoyment — it sets an expectation that the story then confirms or exceeds. In fact, research by Leavitt and Christenfeld (2011) showed that spoiled stories are actually preferred — readers enjoy them MORE because they don't have to work to figure out what's happening and can instead appreciate how it happens. Expectations create a framework that enhances the experience.'
choices.feedback: Surprisingly, the data supports B. Expectations don't diminish experience — they frame it. The same coffee tastes better in an expensive cup. The same wine tastes better from a $50 bottle. The same story is more enjoyable when you know the ending.

choices.text: 'Friend A is right. Surprise is the essence of narrative. Once you know what happens, the mystery is gone. The emotional impact of a plot twist requires not knowing it's coming. Expectation can enhance some experiences, but narrative surprise is different from wine or coffee.'
choices.feedback: Intuitively appealing, but the data doesn't support it. Multiple studies show that spoiled stories are enjoyed more. The twist isn't ruined by knowing it's coming — it's ENHANCED because you can see the setup and appreciate the craftsmanship.

This has implications beyond marketing: placebos work because of expectations; expensive wine tastes better because of expectations; a professor's enthusiasm changes how much students learn. Expectations are not neutral filters — they are active ingredients in experience.

assets.topic: BOSS BATTLE: The Fudge Factor â€” Why Honest People Cheat (But Only a Little)
assets.stage_1_observation: Ariely's Harvard Business School experiment: participants solved 20 simple matrix problems (find two numbers that add up to 10) in 5 minutes. Control group: submitted their worksheet â€” averaged 3.5 correct. Cheating group A: self-checked against an answer key, then reported their score â€” averaged 6.2. Cheating group B: self-checked, shredded their worksheet, and took payment from a jar â€” averaged 6.1. The result: people cheated, but only by a little â€” regardless of how easy it was to cheat without detection.
assets.stage_1_question: Why did participants cheat 'only a little' instead of claiming the maximum possible score? And why did eliminating all risk of detection (shredding the worksheet, taking money from a jar) not increase cheating?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Because dishonesty is not driven by a rational cost-benefit analysis of getting caught. Instead, people operate with a 'fudge factor' â€” they want to benefit from cheating but also maintain a positive self-image as honest people. The limit is set by how much they can cheat while still feeling honest (the 'personal fudge factor' zone). This explains why eliminating detection risk didn't increase cheating: people were already cheating as much as their self-image allowed. The moral constraint is INTERNAL, not external. The real battle is not between the cheater and the system â€” it's between the cheater and their own self-concept.
assets.stage_2_intervention: After the matrix test, a new group of participants was asked to recall either (A) 10 books they read in high school, or (B) the Ten Commandments, BEFORE taking the test. The book-recall group cheated (avg 4.1 vs control 3.1 correct claimed). The Ten Commandments group did not cheat at all (avg 3.0 â€” identical to honest control). A separate test used the MIT Honor Code: participants who signed 'I understand this study falls under the MIT honor system' before the test did not cheat (avg 3.0), while those who didn't sign claimed 5.5 correct â€” even though MIT has no honor code.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Moral reminders eliminate cheating â€” even when there is no enforcement mechanism and no risk of getting caught. Recalling the Ten Commandments or signing an honor code activates the participant's internal moral standards, making dishonesty incompatible with their self-concept. The key insight: people don't need external enforcement to be honest â€” they just need to be reminded of their own moral standards BEFORE the temptation arises. Once the rationalization process starts, it's too late. This is why honor codes work: they must be signed at the BEGINNING of a task, not at the end (when people have already rationalized their cheating).
assets.boss_battle_explanation: The dishonesty research in this chapter overturns the standard economic model of crime (Becker, 1968) which assumes cheating is a cost-benefit calculation: cheat if benefit > probability of getting caught Ã— penalty. Ariely shows the model is wrong in a crucial way: people cheat when they can rationalize it while still viewing themselves as honest. The 'fudge factor' is the distance between what we can get away with and what we can justify to ourselves. The implications are enormous: most white-collar crime, insurance fraud, tax evasion, and corporate misconduct is not committed by 'bad people' â€” it's committed by ordinary people who have rationalized their dishonesty. The solution is not harsher penalties but moral reminders, honor codes, and systems that make rationalization harder.

assets.topic: Cash vs. Tokens: Why One Step Away from Money Doubles the Cheating Rate
assets.question: Ariely's experiments showed that (1) MIT students would steal Cokes from communal fridges but not cash, and (2) participants cheated twice as much when paid in tokens (exchanged for cash later) vs. direct cash. What psychological mechanism explains why the medium of exchange so dramatically affects honesty?
assets.correct_answer: The key mechanism is 'psychological distance from cash' â€” the further removed a transaction is from actual money, the easier it is to rationalize dishonesty. Cash is concrete: stealing a $1 bill feels like stealing. A Coke feels different: it's 'just a Coke,' not money. Tokens feel like game pieces, not currency â€” even though they are immediately exchangeable for cash. The distance from cash creates a 'moral buffer' that weakens the internal alarm that would normally stop dishonest behavior. This explains why: (1) People commit expense report fraud more easily with corporate cards than with cash. (2) Stock option backdating feels less criminal than embezzlement. (3) Insurance fraud is easier to rationalize ('I'm just getting back what I paid in') than directly stealing. (4) Digital currency and credit cards increase spending AND dishonesty compared to cash. The implication: to reduce dishonesty, bring transactions closer to cash â€” eliminate the moral buffer.

assets.topic: BOSS BATTLE: The Free Lunch â€” Why Behavioral Economics Creates Value That Standard Economics Says Can't Exist
assets.stage_1_observation: Standard economics assumes the 'invisible hand': in free markets, rational individuals pursuing self-interest produce optimal outcomes for everyone. No 'free lunches' exist â€” you can't make someone better off without making someone else worse off. But Ariely's research shows systematic, predictable irrationality: anchoring, the endowment effect, the hot-cold empathy gap, the fudge factor, and dozens of other biases. If people make predictable mistakes, then there ARE free lunches â€” interventions that help people make better decisions without hurting anyone.
assets.stage_1_question: How does Ariely's 'free lunch' concept challenge the fundamental assumption of standard economics, and what does it mean for policy and business?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The 'no free lunch' assumption depends on rational actors making optimal decisions. Once we accept that humans are predictably irrational, the possibility of free lunches emerges: interventions that improve outcomes for everyone by working WITH human psychology rather than against it. Examples include: Save More Tomorrow (employees save more without feeling the pain), mandatory cooling-off periods (consumers make better purchase decisions), default enrollment in retirement plans (dramatically increases participation without restricting choice), and moral reminders at the point of decision (reduces dishonesty without enforcement). These are 'free' because they create net benefits â€” higher savings, better health, more satisfaction â€” without requiring anyone to sacrifice. The economist's objection ('if it were so beneficial, people would already do it') fails because people are not the rational calculators economics assumes.
assets.stage_2_intervention: You are advising a government on reducing obesity. Standard economic approach: tax unhealthy foods (makes people pay the true social cost). 'Free lunch' behavioral approach: change cafeteria layouts to put healthy options at eye level, use smaller plates, make unhealthy options less convenient (opt-in rather than opt-out). Which works better and why?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: The behavioral approach can achieve the same or better results without the political and welfare costs of taxation. A tax works by making unhealthy food more expensive, which works for rational consumers but hurts low-income people disproportionately and triggers reactance (people resent being told what to eat). Choice architecture â€” rearranging the decision environment to make healthy choices easier â€” preserves freedom while leveraging predictable irrationality. People still choose freely, but the default is now healthy. Studies show cafeteria rearrangements increase healthy choices by 25-30% with zero resentment. This IS the free lunch: better health outcomes without anyone feeling worse off. Standard economics says this can't happen; behavioral economics shows it does every day.
assets.boss_battle_explanation: The 'free lunch' concept is the rallying cry of behavioral economics. It transforms the field from a critique of standard economics ('look at all these irrational things people do!') into a constructive toolkit for improving human welfare. The free lunches are everywhere once you look: automatic enrollment in retirement plans, organ donation opt-out systems, calorie labeling, simplified enrollment in benefit programs, smart defaults for everything from privacy settings to insurance choices. Each intervention creates value by helping people's rational 'planner' selves constrain their impulsive 'doer' selves. The ultimate insight: people don't need more information or more choices â€” they need environments designed for the humans they actually are, not the rational androids economics imagined.

assets.visual_frame_description: A hospital ward frozen mid-procedure: a nurse's hand hovers over a bandage while red tags pop over each assumption - 'sharp spike is kinder,' 'order doesn't matter' - and a pain-meter line graphs the patient's true agony against the nurses' theory.
assets.player_mission: Walk through the burn ward's daily bath procedure and autopsy every decision the nurses made: the quick-pull tactic, the pain-spike theory, the start-at-the-worst-part plan. For each choice, identify the bias that produced it and redesign the procedure using the evidence the nurses never had.
key_concepts: An explosion of a large magnesium flare left 70 percent of Ariely's body covered with third-degree burns when he was an eighteen-year-old Israeli
The next three years found Ariely wrapped in bandages in a hospital, emerging in a tight synthetic suit and mask that made him look like a crooked version of Spider-Man
The nurses routinely grabbed a bandage and ripped it off as fast as possible, theorizing that a sharp spike of pain was preferable to a slow pull that would extend the treatment
Ariely's experiments showed people feel less pain if treatments such as bandage removal are carried out with lower intensity and longer duration than with high intensity and a shorter duration
Etty, Ariely's favorite nurse, pointed out that pulling bandages quickly might shorten the nurses' own torment when their patients screamed in agony
Even with their vast experience, the nurses were victims of inherent biases in their perceptions of the patients' pain - biases that experience apparently did not alter

A class on the physiology of the brain taught by Professor Hanan Frenk showed Ariely that science is an empirical endeavor in which anyone can propose alternative theories as long as they find empirical ways to test them
Ariely probed pain with heat, cold water, pressure, loud sounds, and even the psychological pain of losing money in the stock market
Behavioral economics, also called judgment and decision making (JDM), draws on aspects of both psychology and economics
For social scientists, experiments are like microscopes or strobe lights: they slow human behavior down, isolate individual forces, and let us test directly what makes us tick
Our irrational behaviors are neither random nor senseless - they are systematic, and since we repeat them again and again, predictable

assets.topic: Dialogue: The Burn Ward Roundtable
assets.visual_frame_description: A hospital conference room where two screens face off: on one side the nurses defend the fast rip while a scream-o-meter spikes, on the other Ariely's line graphs show lower total pain for slow removal.
assets.player_mission: Play the nurses, then switch and play young Ariely as he presents his slow-pull findings to the ward. Argue the quick-pull case from the nurses' own torment and the fear of anticipating pain, then counter with the data on intensity, duration, and the pain of the patients - and decide whether the ward changes its methods.
key_concepts: The nurses had theorized that a vigorous tug at the bandages, causing a sharp spike of pain, was preferable to a slow pulling that would extend the treatment
Ariely concluded that people feel less pain if treatments are carried out with lower intensity and longer duration than with high intensity and a shorter duration
The nurses' theories gave no consideration to the fear the patient felt anticipating the treatment, the fluctuations of pain over time, or the benefit of knowing the pain would be reduced over time
Etty admitted their understanding had been lacking and said the methods should change, but noted the psychological pain the nurses experienced when patients screamed in agony
In the end the procedures were changed, and some of the nurses followed Ariely's recommendations
The episode impressed on Ariely that if experienced nurses misunderstood reality for patients they cared about, other people likely misunderstand the consequences of their behaviors too
Behavioral economics is a relatively new field that draws on aspects of both psychology and economics
The rational economic model is the basic assumption that most economists and many of us hold: that we are capable of making the right decisions for ourselves
Traditional economics holds that if we make a mistake, market forces will sweep down on us and set us back on the path of rationality
Ariely's irrational behaviors are neither random nor senseless but systematic, and since we repeat them again and again, predictable
Each chapter of the book is based on experiments that illustrate a general principle, providing insight into how we think in many contexts of life

assets.topic: Audit: The Predictable-Pattern Field Log
assets.visual_frame_description: A personal dashboard feeds a scrolling ledger: every logged decision gets stamped with its bias - dessert-cart amnesia, price placebo, impulse buy - while a counter-tactic shelf lights up with options.
assets.player_mission: Spend a day logging your own decisions and tag each one with the irrational pattern behind it: the diet promise lost to the dessert cart, the aspirin priced at 50 cents, the impulse purchase. For every entry, note the systematic mistake and design one countermeasure you could actually use.
key_concepts: Ariely asks why we so often promise ourselves to diet, only to have the thought vanish when the dessert cart rolls by
A one-cent aspirin does not cure a headache the way the same aspirin at 50 cents does, showing price itself changes the experienced effect
People who have been asked to recall the Ten Commandments tend to be more honest, at least immediately afterward, than those who haven't
Honor codes actually do reduce dishonesty in the workplace
The nurses' quick-pull method was not due to maliciousness, stupidity, or neglect but to inherent biases in their perceptions of patients' pain
Ariely's research showed that people feel less pain if treatments are carried out with lower intensity and longer duration
The three years Ariely spent observing daily activities as an outsider taught him to reflect on the goals of behaviors, his own and those of others
Understanding the impact of the Ten Commandments in curbing dishonesty might help prevent the next Enron-like fraud
Understanding the dynamics of impulsive eating has implications for every other impulsive decision, including why it's so hard to save money for a rainy day
The value of an experiment lies in extrapolation: the lessons apply not only in the experiment's environment but in many contexts of life
Ariely suggests pausing at the end of each chapter to consider whether the principles revealed might make your life better or worse

assets.topic: Discrimination Matrix: Rationality x Irrationality x Predictability
assets.visual_frame_description: A courtroom-style grid where episode cards slide into cells; the rational column glows faintly while the predictable-irrational column blazes, each card pinned with its experimental evidence.
assets.player_mission: Sort a grid of 12 everyday episodes - the dessert cart, the 50-cent aspirin, the honor code, the failed bandage theory - by whether they fit the rational economic model or systematic irrationality, and by whether the outcome is predictable. Mark each cell with the evidence and name the force that drives it.
key_concepts: In conventional economics, the assumption that we are all rational implies that we compute the value of all options and follow the best possible path of action
Traditional economics holds that market forces will sweep down on irrational decision makers and swiftly set them back on the path of rationality
Ariely argues we are really far less rational than standard economic theory assumes
Our irrational behaviors are systematic, and since we repeat them again and again, predictable
Behavioral economics draws on aspects of both psychology and economics and is also called judgment and decision making (JDM)
Experiments are like microscopes or strobe lights, slowing human behavior to a frame-by-frame narration so individual forces can be examined
The nurses' mistaken theory showed that even experts with vast experience can hold wrong beliefs that were never scientifically tested
Ariely's finding that slow bandage removal hurts less overall contradicts the nurses' quick-pull belief
The 50-cent aspirin cures a headache that a one-cent aspirin cannot, illustrating that price shapes perceived effectiveness
Honor codes reduce dishonesty in the workplace, and recalling the Ten Commandments makes people more honest
Each chapter's experiment illustrates a general principle that applies by extrapolation to many contexts of life
Recognizing where we depart from the ideal of perfect reasoning promises many practical benefits for everyday decisions

assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Rational-Economist Showdown
assets.visual_frame_description: An economics lecture hall turned arena: the rational model stands on a gilded platform that cracks with each experiment you cite, while a banner overhead slowly rewrites itself from 'rational actor' to 'predictably irrational.'
assets.player_mission: Face a defender of the rational economic model who claims market forces will always correct our mistakes. Fire your empirical counter-evidence from the burn ward, the Ten Commandments, and the price of aspirin, and land the knockout point: irrationality is systematic, repeated, and predictable.
key_concepts: The rational economic model is the simple and compelling idea that we are capable of making the right decisions for ourselves
Generations of economists since Adam Smith have built far-reaching conclusions on the assumption of rationality
Traditional economics answers mistakes with market forces that will sweep down and set us back on the path of rationality
Ariely's research shows we are far less rational than standard economic theory assumes
Our irrational behaviors are systematic and, since we repeat them again and again, predictable
The nurses in the burn unit had vast experience yet held a theory about pain that was never scientifically tested and was wrong
Ariely found that lower-intensity, longer-duration treatments hurt less overall than the nurses' quick-pull method
A 50-cent aspirin cures a headache that a one-cent aspirin leaves in place
Recalling the Ten Commandments makes people more honest, and honor codes reduce dishonesty in the workplace
Behavioral economics draws on psychology and economics and aims to move economics away from naive psychology toward empirical scrutiny
Experiments allow social scientists to isolate individual forces and test unambiguously what makes us tick
Understanding how we are predictably irrational provides a starting point for improving decision making and changing the way we live for the better

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: The Decoy Detection Lab
assets.visual_frame_description: A marketplace diorama where each display freezes and the decoy glows in a pulsing red ring while an arrow shows which option it inflates - the Economist trio, the television row, and the menu all at once.
assets.player_mission: Scan 12 product and price displays and spot the decoy in each: the print-only subscription, the colonial needing a roof, the overpriced bread machine, the distorted face. Name what the decoy makes look good, and explain how it changes the choice even though nobody picks it.
key_concepts: The Economist offered an Internet-only subscription for $59, a print-only subscription for $125, and a print-and-Internet subscription for $125
Humans rarely choose things in absolute terms - we don't have an internal value meter, so we focus on the relative advantage of one thing over another
Among 100 students at MIT's Sloan School, 16 chose the Internet-only subscription, zero chose print-only, and 84 chose the print-and-Internet combination
Without the print-only decoy, 68 students chose the Internet-only option for $59 and only 32 chose the combination - the mere presence of the decoy had shifted the choices
Sam the television salesman prices the set he most wants to sell as the middle option because, given three choices, most people will take the middle choice
Restaurant consultant Gregg Rapp found that high-priced entrees boost revenue even if no one buys them, because people order the second most expensive dish
A decoy option that is clearly worse than one alternative but similar to it makes that alternative look better, not just relative to the decoy but overall
In the dating experiment, participants chose the regular, similar-but-superior person over the other undistorted person 75 percent of the time
Williams-Sonoma's $275 bread machine sold poorly until a larger model priced about 50 percent higher was added; then sales of the smaller machine began to rise
When choosing among three houses, buyers pick the colonial with the good roof over the contemporary because the roof-needing colonial makes the comparison easy
Envy and jealousy spring from comparing our lot with others, which is why the Ten Commandments warned against coveting a neighbor's possessions
Most people will walk 15 minutes to save $7 on a $25 pen but not to save $7 on a $455 suit, even though $7 is $7 in both cases

assets.topic: Dialogue: The Economist Subscription Interrogation
assets.visual_frame_description: A British office with a chalkboard showing the two price ladders; each time the decoy is erased, a crowd of student avatars visibly migrates from the $125 bundle to the $59 web deal.
assets.player_mission: Sit in the Economist's London office and interrogate the marketers about the three subscription offers, then switch sides and play the MIT students choosing between them. Run the decoy experiment yourself: show the set with and without the print-only option and watch the 84/16 split become 32/68.
key_concepts: The Economist's marketing wizards knew that humans rarely choose things in absolute terms but focus on the relative advantage of one thing over another
The print-and-Internet option at $125 was clearly better than the print-only option at $125, making the combination a no-brainer
Given the three options, 84 of 100 MIT Sloan students chose the print-and-Internet combination and 16 the Internet-only option
Removing the print-only decoy changed the result to 68 for the Internet-only option and 32 for the combination
The mere presence of the decoy, even though no one selected it, was enough to change the students' choices - a predictably irrational result
Sam the salesman knows that given three choices, most people will take the middle choice, so he prices the television he wants to sell in the middle
Gregg Rapp found that an expensive dish lures customers into ordering the second most expensive choice, which can be engineered for higher profit
Adding an option like -Rome (Rome without free breakfast) makes Rome with free breakfast look better than the difficult-to-compare Paris option
In the photo experiment, the slightly distorted version of a face pushed participants to prefer the similar but undistorted face 75 percent of the time
The bread machine's larger, 50 percent more expensive sibling model gave consumers something to compare, and the smaller machine began to sell
A decoy friend with your basic physical characteristics but slightly less attractive (-you) makes you look better at a singles event
When a similar but better-looking friend of the same sex asks you out for a night, you might wonder whether you're being used as a decoy

assets.topic: Audit: The Relative-Value Field Log
assets.visual_frame_description: A city street overlaid with floating comparison brackets linking every product to its neighbor, while a field notebook stamps each observation with its decoy and its target.
assets.player_mission: Walk through a week of choices - the restaurant menu, the electronics display, the open-house circuit - and log every relative judgment you catch yourself making. For each, name the comparison standard, spot any decoy, and record whether the choice was truly about value or about contrast.
key_concepts: Most people don't know what they want unless they see it in context - we don't know what kind of speaker system we like until we hear one that sounds better than the previous one
We always compare jobs with jobs, vacations with vacations, lovers with lovers, and wines with wines
We tend to compare things that are easily comparable and avoid comparing things that cannot be compared easily
A $7 saving on a $25 pen seems worth a 15-minute trip, while the same $7 on a $455 suit does not - yet $7 is $7 no matter how you count it
It is easy to add $200 to a $5,000 catering bill but hard to spend $3,000 on a new leather sofa, even though we spend more time on the sofa than in the car
The more we have, the more we want - James Hong sold his Porsche Boxster and bought a Toyota Prius to shrink his circles of comparison
When CEO pay was made public in 1993, comparisons pushed salaries to skyrocket rather than fall, with the average CEO now making about 369 times the average worker
A young man making almost $300,000 complained about his salary because two coworkers at adjacent desks were making $310,000
Mencken observed that a man's satisfaction with his salary depends on whether he makes more than his wife's sister's husband
We can sometimes control the circles around us - skipping open houses above our means or walking away from the boastful big spender at a reunion
Relativity is everywhere, and we view everything through its lens - the enchantment of meeting a fellow traveler abroad may be limited to the circumstances
A doctor who dreamed of a Nobel Prize for cancer research moved to Wall Street because colleagues' yachts and vacation homes made him feel poor

assets.topic: Discrimination Matrix: Decoy x Target x Choice Shift
assets.visual_frame_description: A laboratory grid where decoy cards insert into each row and the target column pulses; a readout beside each row shows the before-and-after choice percentages.
assets.player_mission: Complete a grid for 12 decoy scenarios - the Economist trio, the three houses, the distorted faces, the bread machines - by naming the target option each decoy inflates and the measured shift in choices. Mark whether the decoy was ever selected and still moved the market.
key_concepts: The print-only subscription for $125 was the decoy that made the print-and-Internet subscription for $125 look clearly superior
With the decoy present, 84 of 100 MIT students chose the combination; with it removed, only 32 did
The decoy option was chosen by zero of the 100 students, yet its mere presence determined their choices
Adding a clearly inferior option (-A) similar to (A) makes (A) look better overall, not just relative to the decoy
The colonial needing a new roof is the decoy that steers buyers to the colonial with the good roof instead of the contemporary
In the dating experiment, the slightly distorted decoy face made participants prefer the similar but undistorted face 75 percent of the time
The larger, 50 percent more expensive bread machine was never the best seller, but it made the smaller machine start flying off the shelves
Gregg Rapp's expensive menu entrees are decoys that push diners to the second most expensive dish
Sam the salesman places the television he wants to sell in the middle of three options because most customers take the middle choice
The decoy effect helps decide whom to date and marry, and even applies to the honeymoon choice between Rome and Paris
The Economist's marketers assumed the Web reader would otherwise pick the Internet-only option, so they built a decoy to push him to the bundle
Bring a slightly less attractive friend (-you) to a singles event and you will look better in comparison with everyone around

assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Runway-Lights Gauntlet
assets.visual_frame_description: A dark landing strip at night: every product on sale glows as a runway light, but decoys flicker red and the circle illusion shrinks and swells on the horizon as you approach.
assets.player_mission: Pilot your decision-making past the decoys of a full day's shopping while the relativity of the circle illusion shifts around you. Resist the middle-television trap, the $125 combo lure, and the $310,000 desk envy - and land your choices on the runway lights you chose, not the ones the marketers placed.
key_concepts: Like an airplane pilot landing in the dark, we want runway lights on either side of us to guide our choices
The middle circle appears to shrink among larger circles and grow among smaller ones, though it stays the same size - mirroring how the mind compares everything around us
The Economist's print-only decoy sent 84 of 100 MIT students to the $125 combination; without it, 68 chose the $59 Internet-only option
The decoy effect works even though no one ever selects the decoy itself
Sam the television salesman prices the set he wants to sell in the middle because most customers take the middle choice
In the photo experiment, participants preferred the similar-but-superior face 75 percent of the time when the distorted decoy was present
The Williams-Sonoma bread machine began selling only after a larger, 50 percent more expensive model gave consumers a comparison
A young man making almost $300,000 was unhappy because his coworkers made $310,000 - envy is relativity at work
Publicizing CEO pay in 1993 made salaries skyrocket instead of fall, with the average CEO now making about 369 times the average worker
Most people would walk 15 minutes to save $7 on a $25 pen but not to save $7 on a $455 suit, even though $7 is $7
The only cure for the cycle of relativity is to break it - James Hong sold his Boxster and bought a Prius to make his circles of comparison smaller
We can choose smaller circles: skip open houses above our means, and step away from the boastful big spender at the class reunion

chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Fallacy of Supply and Demand

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: The Anchor Hunt
assets.visual_frame_description: A bungee-cord visualization: each product price glows as a peg in the ground while a cord stretches from it to every future price, showing how far the anchor can pull.
assets.player_mission: Hunt for anchors across 12 buying scenarios - the social security digits, the Cotes du Rhone auction, the LCD television, the new-city housing market. Name the anchor in each, say whether it is arbitrary or earned, and predict how it will bend the next bid.
key_concepts: Konrad Lorenz showed goslings imprint on the first moving object they see and stick with that decision - and humans similarly accept the first price they encounter as an anchor
In the MIT auction, students wrote down the last two digits of their social security numbers before bidding, and those digits anchored their willingness to pay
Any question could have created the anchor - the researchers could have asked for the current temperature or the manufacturer's suggested retail price instead
Price tags by themselves are not anchors; they become anchors when we contemplate buying a product or service at that particular price
People who move to a new city generally remain anchored to the prices they paid for housing in their former city
In the annoying-sounds experiment, the group first offered 10 cents demanded an average of 33 cents to hear the sound again, while the 90-cents group demanded 73 cents
The first anchor predominated across all phases of the sound experiment, even when new anchors of 50 cents and flipped 90/10 cents were suggested
Self-herding happens when we believe something is good on the basis of our own previous behavior - each Starbucks visit lines us up behind ourselves
Once the first decision is made, later decisions follow in what seems a logical and coherent manner - the die is cast and the anchor set
The poetical reading auction showed anchors can even flip the sign: students anchored to paying offered about a dollar or two, while those anchored to being paid demanded $1.30 to $4.80
In the real world, anchoring comes from MSRPs, advertised prices, promotions, and product introductions - all supply-side variables
Our sensitivity to price changes might be largely a result of our memory for past prices and our desire for coherence with past decisions

assets.topic: Dialogue: The Gosling Imprinting Trial
assets.visual_frame_description: A lecture hall where the last two digits of each student's social security number float above their heads and their bids rise in price bars that sort themselves by digit size.
assets.player_mission: Re-enact the wine auction with the MIT marketing class: hand out the forms, have the students write their social security digits, collect the yes-no answers and the real bids, then switch sides and watch the 216-to-346-percent spread appear. Interrogate the students about whether their digits influenced them.
key_concepts: Students with social security numbers ending in the upper 20 percent placed bids 216 to 346 percent higher than those ending in the lowest 20 percent
The top 20 percent bid an average of $56 for the cordless keyboard while the bottom 20 percent bid an average of $16
When asked, the students quickly dismissed the suggestion that writing their social security digits had influenced their final bids
Social security numbers were the anchor only because the researchers requested them - any question would have created the anchor
The bids showed coherent logic within categories: everyone was willing to pay more for the keyboard than the trackball and more for the 1996 Hermitage than the 1998 Cotes du Rhone
Arbitrary coherence means initial prices are largely arbitrary, but once established they shape present and future prices for related products
Price tags become anchors only when we contemplate buying a product at that price - the imprint is set at the moment of consideration
In the sounds experiment, the 10-cent group demanded an average of 33 cents while the 90-cent group demanded 73 cents for the same annoying experience
Even after new anchors were suggested, participants stuck with their first anchor across all three phases of the experiment
The poetry auction anchored half the students to paying and half to being paid, producing bids versus demands for the same ambiguous experience
Like Tom Sawyer's whitewashing, an ambiguous experience can be made arbitrarily pleasurable or painful by the anchor set before it
The first decision in a long stream of decisions can have such a long-lasting effect that it percolates into future decisions for years to come

assets.topic: Audit: The First-Decision Ledger
assets.visual_frame_description: A ledger book that fills itself with first-purchase entries, each one growing a chain of later decisions until the page shows a Starbucks queue of your own past selves.
assets.player_mission: Inventory the first decisions that shaped your life - the first Starbucks coffee, the first DVD player, the first apartment rent - and record how each became an anchor for everything that followed. Ask whether the original decision was wise, and note which habits are just self-herding.
key_concepts: Once we buy a new product at a particular price, we become anchored to that price from then on
The first Starbucks visit starts a self-herding process in which each repeat visit lines you up behind your own previous behavior until the coffee becomes a habit
People who move from inexpensive to moderately priced cities spend similar amounts on housing, even if it means squeezing into smaller homes
Renting for about a year in a new location lets you adjust to the new market before making a purchase that aligns with it
The first anchor influences not only the immediate buying decision but many others that follow, like the pull of a bungee cord
Assael anchored his black pearls to the finest gems in the world, and the high prices followed forever after
Howard Schultz designed Starbucks as a continental coffeehouse so that Dunkin' Donuts prices would not serve as the anchor
Starbucks made lateral moves to Caffe Americano, Macchiato, and Frappuccino seem logical once the price bracket was accepted
Descartes said 'I think, therefore I am,' but we might be nothing more than the sum of our first, naive, random behaviors
Train yourself to question repeated behaviors: how did the habit begin, how much pleasure does it deliver, and could the money be better spent
Pay particular attention to the first decision in a long stream of decisions about clothing, food, and other choices
Socrates said the unexamined life is not worth living - it may be time to inventory the imprints and anchors in your own life

assets.topic: Discrimination Matrix: Anchor Source x Product x Bid Outcome
assets.visual_frame_description: A trading floor display where anchor cards connect to product rows and the final bid lights up green when the anchor held and red when it broke.
assets.player_mission: Fill a 12-cell grid matching anchor sources - social security digits, offered prices, MSRP, prior city rent - to products and the resulting bids. Mark which anchors were arbitrary, which held across later offers, and which flipped the direction of willingness to pay.
