key_concepts: The social security digits served as anchors: upper-20 percent endings produced bids 216 to 346 percent higher than the lowest 20 percent
In the sounds experiment, the 10-cent anchor produced 33-cent average demands while the 90-cent anchor produced 73-cent demands for the same sound
The first anchor held through two later phases even when new anchors (50 cents, then flipped 90/10 cents) were introduced
Arbitrary coherence means initial prices are largely arbitrary but shape present and future prices for the item and related products
Price tags become anchors only when we contemplate buying at that price - otherwise they are just numbers
Housing anchors follow people across cities: Lubbock-to-Pittsburgh transplants spend what they spent before, as do Los Angeles transplants
The poetry auction flipped the sign of the exchange: one group bid to pay, the other demanded payment, for the same recitation
The students' relative bids were coherent - everyone paid more for the keyboard than the trackball and more for the better wine
Supply and demand are not independent forces: market prices such as MSRPs and promotions influence consumers' willingness to pay
If people had amnesia for past prices, price changes such as doubling the price of milk would have a trivial effect on demand
In the long run, a doubled gasoline tax would have much less effect on demand than short-term reactions suggest, as new anchors form
Free-market trading assumes we know the value of what we trade, but arbitrary anchors mean trades may not reflect true pleasure

assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Pearl King's Showcase
assets.visual_frame_description: A Fifth Avenue jewelry window glowing at night: a string of black pearls floats among diamonds and rubies while a price tag rises higher and higher, and a crowd of well-dressed admirers multiplies outside.
assets.player_mission: Take the role of Salvador Assael and build the launch that turns unsellable black pearls into luxury icons - or take the role of the buyer who must resist. Set the anchor, pair the pearls with diamonds, rubies, and emeralds, price them outrageously in Harry Winston's Fifth Avenue window, and see how much value you can manufacture from nothing.
key_concepts: Assael's first attempts to sell Tahitian black pearls failed - they were gunmetal gray, about the size of musket balls, and he returned from his trip without a single sale
Assael waited a year for better specimens, then had Harry Winston place them in his Fifth Avenue window with an outrageously high price tag
A full-page advertisement set a string of black pearls among diamonds, rubies, and emeralds in the glossiest of magazines
The pearls that once hung on a rope in the Polynesian sea were soon parading through Manhattan on the necks of the city's most prosperous divas
Mark Twain noted that to make a man covet a thing, it is only necessary to make the thing difficult to attain
Assael anchored his pearls to the finest gems in the world, and the prices followed forever after
Arbitrary coherence: initial prices are largely arbitrary, but once established they shape present and future prices
In the sounds experiment, the first anchor held even when new anchors were suggested - first impressions resonate over long sequences of decisions
The poetry auction showed the same ambiguous experience becomes pleasurable or painful depending on the anchor set beforehand
Starbucks separated itself from Dunkin' Donuts through ambience so that old prices would not be the anchor
Self-herding makes each repeat Starbucks visit feel like acting on genuine preferences until the habit is fixed
Because anchors rather than preferences may determine behavior, free-market trading may not maximize the happiness we derive from goods

chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Cost of Zero Cost

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: The Free! Hazard Sweep
assets.visual_frame_description: A supermarket aisle where every free offer radiates a red glow; a scanner badge over each one reveals the hidden price - the $13 forgone, the 0.5 percent oil-change value, the unwanted DVD player.
assets.player_mission: Sweep 12 offers - free shipping thresholds, buy-two-get-one-free, the free $10 certificate, the free oil change - and flag the FREE! hazard in each. Name what you would really be giving up, compute the true cost, and decide whether to grab or walk.
key_concepts: Zero is not just another price - it is an emotional hot button and a source of irrational excitement
When the Lindt truffle cost 15 cents and the Kiss one cent, 73 percent chose the truffle; with both cut by one cent and the Kiss free, 69 percent chose the free Kiss
The real allure of FREE! is tied to humans' intrinsic fear of loss - choosing a free item carries no visible possibility of a poor decision
In the Halloween experiment, about 70 percent of children chose a free small Snickers bar over the better deal of trading one Kiss for the large bar
Most people at a Boston mall chose a free $10 Amazon gift certificate over a $20 certificate for seven dollars - forgoing a $13 profit
Amazon's French division priced shipping at one franc (about 20 cents) and saw no increase in sales; free shipping produced the same dramatic jump as elsewhere
Ariely bought an Audi partly for free oil changes for three years - about $150 of value, roughly 0.5 percent of the purchase price
Most people would choose a free credit card with a 12 percent APR over a 9 percent APR card with a $100 annual fee, paying much more if they carry a balance
A 'zero calories' label or a calorie-free beer makes people feel they are doing the right thing healthwise, even compared with a three-calorie option
Free items can make perfect sense - a bin of free athletic socks has no downside - but trouble arises when FREE! competes with a better alternative
The difference between two cents and one cent is small, but the difference between one cent and zero is huge
When something is FREE! we forget the downside, because FREE! gives us such an emotional charge that we perceive the offer as immensely more valuable than it is

assets.topic: Dialogue: The Halloween Candy Trade
assets.visual_frame_description: A front porch on Halloween night: two candy bars float in front of a giant trick-or-treater, and the free small bar pulses with a warm glow that outshines the objectively better trade.
assets.player_mission: Play Joey the Spider-Man and then Zoe the princess as Ariely works the porch: the two-Snickers trade where both bars have a cost, then the free small bar versus the trade for the large one. Feel the 70 percent gravity of FREE! and argue both sides of the deal to yourself.
key_concepts: Joey easily traded two of his three Hershey's Kisses for the two-ounce Snickers bar, getting more than six times the return on investment in net chocolate weight
All but one of the kids offered both bars at a cost traded in two Kisses for the bigger candy bar
Zoe was offered a choice between the large Snickers for one Kiss or the small Snickers for free, and the rational calculation clearly favored the trade
About 70 percent of the children in Zoe's condition gave up the better deal and took the worse deal just because it was free
The experiment was repeated with students at the MIT student center and replicated the pattern seen on Halloween
The draw of zero cost is not limited to monetary transactions - whether it's products or money, we can't resist the gravitational pull of FREE!
In the chocolate table experiment, 73 percent chose the truffle at 15 cents versus one cent for the Kiss; when the Kiss became free, 69 percent chose the Kiss
Standard economic theory predicts no change from an equal one-cent discount on both chocolates, but the zero price changed everything
The zero price effect persisted in a cafeteria where chocolates were added to purchases at the cashier line, ruling out a lack of change as the explanation
Because humans are intrinsically afraid of loss, choosing a free item seems risk-free while choosing the paid item risks a poor decision
A $20 gift certificate for seven dollars delivers a $13 profit, yet most mall shoppers jumped for the free $10 certificate
The one-franc shipping bargain in France was virtually ignored, while free shipping caused an enthusiastic response - zero is a different place

assets.topic: Audit: The Zero-Price Audit Trail
assets.visual_frame_description: A receipt tape unspooling across a desk, each free item glowing and a cost-counter beside it ticking up the real price of zero.
assets.player_mission: Audit a month of your own purchases and mark every choice touched by zero: the free checking account, the coupon run, the free museum day, the free gift with purchase. For each entry, compute what free actually cost you in money, time, or unwanted goods.
key_concepts: A free checking account with no benefits may cost more than a five-dollar account that includes free traveler's checks and online billing
A mortgage with no closing costs but off-the-wall interest rates and fees shows how free can hide the real price
Ariely drove about 7,000 miles a year with oil changes needed every 10,000 miles at about $75 each - the free oil was worth about $150 over three years
The free-oil offer's influence on the Audi purchase was, from a rational perspective, unjustifiably large - about 0.5 percent of the purchase price
Zero also applies to time: 45 minutes waiting for a free taste of ice cream is time taken from something else
On free-entrance day the museum is overcrowded with long lines, yet Ariely knows it is a mistake and goes anyway
The pain of paying is relatively insensitive to the amount paid - every additional dollar on a bill pains us less (diminishing sensitivity)
Because the pain of paying is insensitive to amount, one person should pay the whole restaurant bill and friends should take turns paying over time
A $100 bill split four ways costs the table about 40 units of pain, while one person paying the whole bill costs about 26 units
Recalling the Ten Commandments example aside, most people overemphasize the yearly fee and pick the free credit card that costs more in the long run
In the land of pricing, zero is not just another discount - the difference between one cent and zero is huge
Want people to do the right thing? Don't just lower co-pays for colonoscopies and mammograms - make these critical procedures free

assets.topic: Discrimination Matrix: Price Point x Emotion x Choice
assets.visual_frame_description: A laboratory matrix where each price row lights an emotion gauge and a choice column; the zero-price rows all blaze red while the economist's predicted column stays cold and empty.
assets.player_mission: Complete the grid for 12 zero-price cases - chocolates at 15/1 and 14/0 cents, the Amazon franc, AOL's flat rate, the gift certificates - by rating the emotional charge and the choice outcome in each. Mark which cases match standard cost-benefit analysis and which break it.
key_concepts: Standard cost-benefit analysis predicts no change in chocolate choice from an equal one-cent discount, yet the free Kiss took 69 percent of customers
When the Kiss was priced at two cents, one cent, and zero with the truffle at 27, 26, and 25 cents, only the drop to zero produced a dramatic reaction
The zero price effect survived in a cafeteria setting where chocolates were paid for at the cashier, so a lack of change cannot explain it
One franc of shipping (about 20 cents) was a real bargain that French shoppers virtually ignored, while free shipping started a stampede
AOL's flat $19.95 monthly plan produced an overnight jump from 140,000 to 236,000 customers and a doubling of average time online
AOL's customers hit busy phone lines, forcing AOL to lease services from other providers at premium prices
The allure of FREE! is tied to the fear of loss - a free item has no visible possibility of a poor decision
A free $10 gift certificate beat a $20 certificate for seven dollars in most mall shoppers' minds, even though the paid one earns $13
Discounting from two cents to one cent changed nothing; the drop to zero changed everything - zero is in a category all its own
The free-oil offer's worth ($150, about 0.5 percent of the car's price) had an unjustifiably large influence on Ariely's Audi purchase
A zero-calorie beer increases the feeling that you're doing the right thing healthwise, even versus a three-calorie beer
Most people overemphasize a credit card's yearly fee and choose the free 12 percent APR card over the 9 percent card with a $100 annual fee

assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Free-Chocolate Stampede
assets.visual_frame_description: A public building atrium where a crowd of shoppers presses toward a table with a 'One chocolate per customer' sign; the free Kiss tray glows while a whiteboard charts the 73/27 split flipping to 31/69.
assets.player_mission: Stand at the chocolate table as the crowd surges toward the free Kisses: manage the either-or rule, track the 73/27 split flipping to 31/69, and hold the line against the economist who insists nothing changed. Keep the experiment clean to the last customer.
key_concepts: With the truffle at 15 cents and the Kiss at one cent, 73 percent chose the truffle and 27 percent a Kiss
With the truffle at 14 cents and the Kiss free, only 31 percent chose the truffle while 69 percent chose the free Kiss
Both chocolates were discounted by the same amount, so the relative difference and expected pleasure were unchanged - yet behavior reversed
A passing economist following standard cost-benefit theory would say the customers should have chosen the truffles by the same margin
The shoppers were not making a reasoned cost-benefit analysis - they were simply responding to the fact that the Kisses were free
When the Kiss was priced at two, one, and zero cents (with the truffle at 27, 26, and 25 cents), only the drop to zero mattered
Running the promotion at an MIT cafeteria cashier line reproduced the same overwhelming preference for the free option
Most transactions have an upside and a downside, but when something is FREE! we forget the downside
The zero price effect is in a category all its own - nothing beats the emotional surge of FREE!
Seven free DVD titles lured buyers toward a high-definition player locked in a losing format war with Blu-Ray
Free! can drive social policy: eliminate registration and inspection fees to push electric cars, and make colonoscopies and mammograms free
Zero is a different place: the difference between one cent and zero is huge, not like the small difference between two cents and one cent

chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Cost of Social Norms

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: The Norm-Domain Radar
assets.visual_frame_description: A split-screen scanner: friendly favors appear on the warm side, wages and rents on the cold side, and any mention of money draws a crack across the dividing wall.
assets.player_mission: Sweep 12 exchanges - moving a couch, paying rent, the lawyer checking the mail, the $30 hourly offer - and tag each one as social or market on your radar. For each, name what happens if the wrong norm gets introduced: the fine, the price tag on the gift, the tip.
key_concepts: We live simultaneously in two worlds: social norms (friendly requests, warm, no instant payback required) and market norms (wages, prices, rents, comparable benefits, prompt payment)
Offering your mother-in-law payment for Thanksgiving dinner puts a damper on the party and violates the social norm
When market norms enter our considerations, the social norms depart - mentioning money converts a favor into underpaid work
AARP lawyers refused $30 an hour for work with needy retirees but overwhelmingly agreed to do the same work for free
Explicitly pricing a gift - calling it a '50-cent Snickers bar' - moves it into the realm of market norms
In the Israeli day care study, a fine for late pickups replaced the social norm with a market norm, and tardiness actually became a choice parents made
Once a social norm is trumped by a market norm, it rarely returns - social relationships are not easy to reestablish
Gifts are financially inefficient but are an important social lubricant that builds long-term relationships
A $1,000 cash bonus is what most employees would choose, but a $1,000 vacation would build more loyalty and enjoyment of work
Stating the prices of benefits on a paycheck stub changes the workplace from a social environment to a transactional relationship
The sensei replied that if he charged his students for martial arts training, they would not be able to afford him
Police officers, firefighters, and soldiers don't risk their lives for their weekly pay - pride in profession and a sense of duty motivate them

assets.topic: Dialogue: The Thanksgiving Payment Faux Pas
assets.visual_frame_description: A Norman Rockwell-style dining room that freezes as a wallet appears above the turkey; a wine glass tilts, napkins drop, and a thermometer labeled 'relationship' plunges.
assets.player_mission: Replay the Thanksgiving dinner where the guest pulls out his wallet: run the scene first as the offering guest, then as the red-faced mother-in-law, then as the family that watches the silence fall. Rewind and choose the move that keeps the dinner in the social world.
key_concepts: The social norms world is warm and fuzzy, and instant paybacks are not required - you may help move your neighbor's couch without him rushing to move yours
The market norms world is sharp-edged: wages, prices, rents, interest, and costs-and-benefits, where you get what you pay for
Offering direct payment for the Thanksgiving dinner makes the mother-in-law stand up red-faced and ruins the occasion
When social and market norms collide, trouble sets in - as when a dating man starts counting what the romance is costing him
Woody Allen's immortal words: 'The most expensive sex is free sex'
In the circle-dragging experiment, the $5 group dragged 159 circles, the 50-cent group dragged 101, and the unpaid favor group dragged 168
The unpaid participants applied social norms and worked more than the low-paid group and slightly more than the $5 group
When money was mentioned, the 50-cent participants switched to market norms, decided 50 cents wasn't much, and worked halfheartedly
The AARP lawyers refused $30 an hour for needy retirees but overwhelmingly agreed to provide the same services free
Gifts keep exchanges in the social world - small gifts offend no one, and even small gifts keep us away from market norms
Mention what a gift cost you, and you will see the back of people faster than you can say market norms
Recovering a social relationship after introducing market norms is difficult - the mother-in-law will remember the incident for years

assets.topic: Audit: The Social-Market Ledger
assets.visual_frame_description: A double-column ledger book: warm entries fill the social side, sharp entries the market side, and any item that crosses the middle leaves a scorch mark.
assets.player_mission: Keep a week-long ledger of every favor, gift, payment, and fee in your life, and classify each as social or market exchange. Flag the transitions - the priced gift, the late fee, the mention of cost - and note which relationships took damage.
key_concepts: Social norms include friendly requests like 'Could you help me move this couch?' with no instant payback required
Market relationships are not necessarily evil - they include self-reliance, inventiveness, and individualism - but they imply comparable benefits and prompt payments
In the circle-dragging experiment, $5 produced 159 circles, 50 cents produced 101, and no money at all produced 168
Replacing cash with gifts kept everyone in the social world: Snickers 162 circles, Godiva 169, and nothing at all 168
Explicitly pricing the gift as a '50-cent Snickers bar' dropped effort to the level of 50 cents in cash
The AARP lawyers refused $30 an hour but accepted the same work free - zero dollars was more attractive than $30
Thinking about money makes people more self-reliant and less helpful, as Vohs, Mead, and Goode's scrambled-sentence experiments showed
The money-primed group waited about five and a half minutes before asking for help on a puzzle, versus about three minutes for the neutral group
Asking a friend to help move a large piece of furniture is fine, but asking him to work beside paid movers is not
Asking your lawyer neighbor to bring in your mail is fine, but asking him to prepare a rental contract free is not
Companies that treat customers like family must maintain the social relationship under all circumstances - one violation sends consumers back to market exchange
Money is very often the most expensive way to motivate people; social norms are not only cheaper but often more effective

assets.topic: Discrimination Matrix: Reward x Norm x Effort
assets.visual_frame_description: A spreadsheet-style arena where each reward card slides into its column and a circle-counter animates 159, 101, 168, 162, and the collapse back to the 50-cent level.
assets.player_mission: Fill the grid mapping reward types - $5, 50 cents, nothing, a Snickers bar, a priced Snickers bar, Godiva - to the norm each triggers and the circles dragged in the experiment. Mark which rewards kept participants in the social world and which pushed them into the market.
key_concepts: Five dollars produced 159 circles, 50 cents produced 101, and no money produced 168 - people worked harder under social norms than for 50 cents
A Snickers bar (worth about 50 cents) produced 162 circles and Godiva chocolates (worth about five dollars) produced 169 - gifts kept participants in the social world
Calling the reward a '50-cent Snickers bar' dropped effort to the same level as 50 cents in cash - the priced gift entered the market realm
For market norms to emerge, it is sufficient to mention money, even when no money changes hands
The AARP lawyers said no to $30 an hour but yes to free work - once market norms entered, the social norms departed
The day care fine turned tardiness into a purchasable option, and lateness persisted even after the fine was removed
In the money-priming experiments, participants unscrambling money-related sentences asked for help later, helped less, and chose seats farther away from teammates
The money-primed participants showed the characteristics of the market: more selfish, more self-reliant, and wanting more time alone
The salary group wanted to select tasks requiring individual input rather than teamwork
Gifts are financially inefficient - a $50 bottle of Bordeaux may be worth at most $25 to the recipient - but they build social relationships
Explicitly stating the financial value of benefits on a paycheck stub diminishes enjoyment, motivation, and loyalty
Open-source communities like Linux show how social rewards and reputation strongly motivate behavior without money

assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Day Care Fine Reversal
assets.visual_frame_description: A day care yard at dusk: a fine schedule is posted, then torn down, while a clock tower shows late pickups climbing - and a ghostly outline of the old social contract fades from the wall.
assets.player_mission: Run the Israeli day care center: introduce the late-pickup fine, watch the parents turn tardy, then remove it and confront the truth that the social norm never comes back. Decide whether to reintroduce guilt, and manage the wrecked social contract.
key_concepts: Before the fine, the teachers and parents had a social contract, and parents who were late felt guilty and became more prompt
Once the fine was imposed, the day care had inadvertently replaced social norms with market norms - parents could decide whether to be late and often chose to be late
The fine did not work well as a deterrent and had long-term negative effects
When the fine was removed, parents' behavior didn't change - they continued to pick up their kids late, with a slight increase in tardy pickups
When a social norm collides with a market norm, the social norm goes away for a long time
Social relationships are not easy to reestablish - once the bloom is off the rose, it will rarely return
In the circle-dragging experiment, unpaid participants working as a favor dragged more circles (168) than the 50-cent group (101)
AARP lawyers refused $30 an hour for needy retirees but overwhelmingly accepted the same work for free
A gift, even a small one, is sufficient to get people to help - but mention what the gift cost and they walk away
Companies can't have it both ways: they can't treat customers like family one moment and impersonally the next
Cutting benefits like medical coverage converts the employer-employee social relationship into a market relationship, and 'corporate loyalty' becomes an oxymoron
Money is very often the most expensive way to motivate people - social norms are not only cheaper, but often more effective

chapters.title: Chapter 5: The Power of a Free Cookie

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: The Selfishness Thermometer
assets.visual_frame_description: A candy booth where every offer lights a selfishness thermometer: the penny trays run hot, the free trays glow cool, and the communal sushi plate sits untouched with one piece left.
assets.player_mission: Scan 12 sharing scenarios - the free cookie box, the communal sushi plate, the one-cent Starbursts, the free truffle tray - and read the selfishness level in each. Name the norm at work and predict how many units each person takes.
key_concepts: At Filene's Basement's 'Running of the Brides,' about a thousand brides-to-be trampled one another in a mass grab for discount wedding dresses, showing rampant selfishness
When money is added to a situation governed by social norms, the added payment can reduce motivation - '$3 for your help?' turns a favor into underpaid work
In the Susan-the-baker thought experiment, free cookies make you think about social justice and coworkers' welfare, while nickel cookies let you take as many as you want
At the Starburst booth, about 58 students per hour bought candy at a cent each, while 207 per hour took candy when it was free - nearly three times as many
Average candies per customer fell from 3.5 at one cent to 1.1 when free - almost all students politely took exactly one Starburst
When price is not part of the exchange, we become less selfish maximizers and start caring more about the welfare of others
The communal plate transforms food into a shared resource and leads us into the realm of social norms and sharing rules
The sushi waitress said she finds one extra piece left almost every time - more common than people finishing all their sushi
In the effort experiment, the monetary group took an average of 30 truffles, the free group 1.5, and the effort group 8.6
When prices are zero and social norms are part of the equation, people look at the world as a communal good
A $3 offer for a tire change changes your perspective: you look at the situation as work and conclude it is not worth your time
Effort falls somewhere in the middle of the spectrum between market and social norms, keeping a large part of the social norms intact

assets.topic: Dialogue: The Susan Cookie Stand
assets.visual_frame_description: An office corridor where the free cookie box glows warmly and each taker politely lifts one, while the nickel version of the same box turns the taker into a hoarder with a full basket.
assets.player_mission: Play Susan the baker walking the office with a hundred cookies, then play the coworker she visits: first the free offer where you weigh hunger, waistline, and coworkers, then the nickel-apiece offer where you stock up without compunction. Feel the norm switch and narrate it out loud.
key_concepts: With free cookies, you consider your hunger, your waistline, your love of chocolate-chip-oatmeal cookies, and how coworkers would feel if the cookies ran out
When Susan asks a nickel apiece, you take a bunch to eat and take home without compunction, not thinking about depriving your coworkers
By asking for money, Susan introduced market norms into the equation, chasing away the social norms that governed the free cookies
Once money is introduced into the exchange, you stop thinking about what's socially right and wrong and simply maximize your cookie intake
In economic exchanges, we are perfectly selfish and unfair, and we think following our wallets is the right thing to do
When the price is not part of an exchange, we start caring about the welfare of others and limit consumption
At the Starburst booth, the free condition drew 207 students per hour versus 58 in the monetary condition - but each took far fewer candies
Average Starbursts per customer dropped from 3.5 at one cent to 1.1 when free, with almost all students taking exactly one
Students collectively took fewer Starbursts as the price decreased from one cent to free - the opposite of the second law of demand
We are caring social animals, but when the rules of the game involve money, this tendency is muted
In the truffle experiment, the monetary group took an average of 30 truffles while the free group took a polite 1.5
Not mentioning prices ushers in social norms, and with those social norms, we start caring more about others

assets.topic: Audit: The Communal-Resource Field Log
assets.visual_frame_description: A kitchen counter diary: each shared dish logs its takers' counts in floating numbers - 1, 1, 1 on the free shelf, 3.5, 3.5, 3.5 next to the penny jar.
assets.player_mission: Log a week of communal resources - the office snack shelf, the shared birthday cake, the last olive, the sushi plate - and record how many units you took and the rule you used. For each entry, note whether price was part of the exchange and how that changed your ethics.
key_concepts: Taking the last olive when dining out with friends feels like such a big deal because the shared food becomes a social good
At a party, you balance your desire for the Red Velvet cake against the desires of your friends and end up with only a medium-sized slice
When sushi is served on a large plate in the middle of the table, taking the last piece feels 'a bit declassé'
The waitress reported finding one extra piece of sushi left almost every time - more common than people finishing all their sushi
When dining alone or with a personal portion, Ariely always manages to finish everything on the plate
The communal plate transforms food into a shared resource that leads into the realm of social norms and rules for sharing
When Starbursts were free, students limited themselves to an average of 1.1 candies and almost all took exactly one
In the effort experiment, participants took an average of 8.6 truffles in exchange for finding pairs of s's - between the free 1.5 and the monetary 30
Effort keeps a large part of the social norms, though not all of them - it sits on the spectrum between market and social norms
Investing effort rather than cash in recycling, neighborhood watch, kids' schools, and soup kitchens keeps us in the domain of social norms
The more people who stopped for free Starbursts took fewer candies each, so total demand actually decreased as the price went to zero
As social animals we care about others, but when money is part of the game this tendency is muted

assets.topic: Discrimination Matrix: Price x Social Norm x Demand
assets.visual_frame_description: A demand-curve auditorium: the curve climbs steeply from 10 to 5 to 1 cent, then snaps backward at zero while two laws of demand duel on a scoreboard.
assets.player_mission: Fill the 12-cell grid of the truffle and Starburst experiments: price points from 10 cents to free, the people who stopped, the units per person, and total demand. Mark where the first law of demand holds, where the second law fails, and the backward sloping zone.
key_concepts: Dropping chocolate prices from 10 cents to 5 cents increased total demand by about 240 percent, verifying both laws of demand
Dropping prices from 5 cents to 1 cent increased total demand by about 400 percent, verifying both laws of demand
Dropping the price from 1 cent to free verified the first law (more people stopped) but disconfirmed the second (each took less), cutting total demand about 50 percent
The theory of demand is solid except when we're dealing with the price of zero - when price is not part of the exchange, social norms become entangled
At the Starburst booth, 58 students per hour bought at one cent while 207 per hour took when free - nearly three times as many people
Average candies per customer fell from 3.5 at one cent to 1.1 when free, the opposite of the second law of demand
Because more people took fewer candies, students collectively took fewer Starbursts as the price decreased from one cent to free
Economists call the decrease in demand as price falls a 'backward sloping demand curve'
The first law of demand says more women buy Vera Wang gowns at $249 than at $10,000; the second says buyers take multiple units at low prices
Wedding gowns are a case where the second law is less relevant, yet multiple women have been sighted leaving Filene's with more than one gown
In the effort condition, people took an average of 8.6 truffles - between the monetary 30 and the free 1.5 - showing effort keeps part of the social norms
Cap and Trade puts a price on pollution, and once companies pay for the right to pollute, morality and concern for the environment become nonissues

assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Running of the Brides Melee
assets.visual_frame_description: A department store at dawn: brides in bright uniforms surge toward stripped racks, dresses flying like chum, while a slow-motion readout overhead shows selfishness maxing out as emotional intensity peaks.
assets.player_mission: Survive and manage the Running of the Brides: keep the gowns on the racks, hold the line at $249 to $699, and test whether any social norm can survive a thousand brides at peak arousal. Hold the event together and file your verdict on what emotion does to other-regarding behavior.
key_concepts: At Filene's Basement's annual Running of the Brides, gowns originally priced at thousands of dollars are offered for a pittance, from $249 to $699
The minute the doors open, the brides turn into a frantic, screaming, pushing mob, tearing as many dresses as they can carry off the racks
Ariely witnessed rampant selfishness and terrible language, though not much violence, at the event
At $249 instead of $10,000, a Vera Wang gown dramatically increases demand - more women can afford it, and some buy multiple units
In economic exchanges, we are perfectly selfish and unfair, and we think following our wallets is the right thing to do
When you're focused, mind and body, on one highly emotional objective - grabbing that wedding dress - it's hard to factor in others' well-being
For social norms to operate, people cannot be at their most emotionally piqued state - when emotions run high, social norms get trampled
Ariely gave up on fixing the event because getting a bride to concentrate on 'other people' versus a discounted gown seemed nearly impossible
The Starburst experiment showed the flip side: when the price dropped to zero, customers restrained themselves and took far fewer units
Average Starbursts per customer fell from 3.5 at one cent to 1.1 when free, and total demand fell about 50 percent when truffles went from 1 cent to free
In the effort experiment, people took 30 truffles for money, 1.5 when free, and 8.6 for effort - effort keeps a large part of social norms
When price is not part of the exchange, we become less selfish maximizers and start caring more about the welfare of others

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: The Hot-Cold Prediction Switch
assets.visual_frame_description: A darkened Berkeley dorm room where a Saran-wrapped laptop glows on a bed; an arousal meter swings toward the red high zone while two answer columns, cold predictions and hot predictions, split apart on the wall.
assets.player_mission: Move through the nineteen sexual-preference questions, five immorality questions, and five safe-sex questions, tagging each answer as cold-state or hot-state. Spot which numbers balloon under arousal - sexual preferences up 72 percent, immoral intent up 136 percent, condom skipping up 25 percent - and judge whether any cold-state forecast survives contact with the red zone of the arousal meter.
key_concepts: In 2001 Ariely and George Loewenstein studied how rational, intelligent people predict their attitudes when in an impassioned state, using 25 male Berkeley students
Participants answered questions in a cold, rational state and later while aroused by erotic pictures and masturbation, using a Saran-wrapped laptop and a 12-key keypad
Across 19 questions about sexual preferences, aroused participants predicted their desire to engage in odd sexual activities would be 72 percent higher than they predicted when cold
On five questions about immoral behaviors like date rape, aroused participants predicted their propensity more than twice as high - 136 percent higher - than in the cold state
Despite years of warnings about condoms, participants were 25 percent more likely in the aroused state to predict they would forego condoms
The idea of sexual contact with an animal was more than twice as appealing when aroused (16) as when cold (6), a 167 percent difference
The willingness to slip a woman a drug to increase the chance of sex rose from 5 percent cold to 26 percent aroused, a 420 percent difference
Keeping trying to have sex after a date said no rose from 20 percent cold to 45 percent aroused, a 125 percent difference
Prevention, protection, conservatism, and morality disappeared completely from the radar screen when participants were aroused
The participants revealed in their unaroused state that they themselves did not know what they were like once aroused
Our inability to understand ourselves in a different emotional state does not seem to improve with experience, even for a familiar emotion like sexual arousal
A teenager driving alone is 40 percent more likely to get into an accident than an adult; with one other teenager the rate doubles, and with a third teenager it doubles again

assets.topic: Dialogue: The Dr. Jekyll Test
assets.visual_frame_description: A split-screen dorm room: on the left a calm Roy doing homework under lamplight, on the right a flushed Roy clicking the arousal meter to its bright red high zone as a question pops up on the Saran-wrapped screen.
assets.player_mission: Interrogate Roy, the affable straight-A biology major who plays Chopin etudes, about his decisions in both states: first the cold, superego-driven answers, then the hot answers given while the arousal meter sits in the red zone. Catch the moment his self-understanding collapses, and press him on whether 'Just say no' can possibly hold when passion takes over.
key_concepts: Roy was typical of the 25 participants: accomplished, intelligent, and kind, with straight A's, the volleyball team captaincy, and a steady girlfriend
In the cold state the participants respected women, were not attracted to odd sexual activities, took the moral high ground, and expected to always use a condom
In the aroused state, prevention, protection, conservatism, and morality vanished from the participants' decisions
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde in 1885 after a nightmare, capturing the Victorian fascination with repressive propriety versus uncontrollable passion
The experiment revealed not just the old story that we are all like Jekyll and Hyde, but that every one of us, regardless of how good we are, underpredicts the effect of passion on behavior
MIT's Sloan School stymied the project with a committee consisting mostly of women; Walter Bender, head of the Media Lab, approved it
The ads posted around Sproul Plaza sought male heterosexual participants 18 and over, offered $10 per session, and warned the experiments could involve sexually arousing material
The committee worried about participants uncovering repressed memories of sexual abuse or discovering they were sex addicts, even though any student with a computer could find graphic pornography
'Just say no' assumes we can turn off passion at will, an assumption the study showed to be false
Avoiding temptation altogether is easier than overcoming it once it has started to lure us in
Sex education should focus less on the physiology and biology of the reproductive system and more on strategies to deal with the emotions that accompany sexual arousal
Before the birth of their first child, Sumi plunged her hands into a bucket of ice for two minutes and afterward clearly understood the appeal of an epidural

assets.topic: Audit: The Emotional-State Field Log
assets.visual_frame_description: A city street at dusk where each decision scene floats in a bubble tagged cold-plan or hot-outcome; a giant ledger column records the gap while a Jekyll-and-Hyde mask rotates overhead.
assets.player_mission: Audit ten real-world decisions from the chapter - condom carrying, teenage speeding, epidurals, angry e-mails, sports-car contracts - and classify each as a cold-state plan or a hot-state outcome. Log the gap between predicted and actual behavior for each, then propose a precautionary device that could be configured in a cold state to foil the hot state.
key_concepts: To make informed decisions we need to somehow experience and understand the emotional state we will be in at the other side of the experience
When the boss criticizes us publicly, we might be tempted to send a vehement e-mail, but we would be better off putting the reply in the draft folder for a few days
After test-driving a sports car, we should take a break and discuss the spouse's plan to buy a minivan before signing a contract
We promise to save for retirement but spend the money on a vacation; we vow to diet but surrender to the dessert cart
Giving up on long-term goals for immediate gratification is procrastination
Precautionary devices configured in a cold state, like a modified OnStar system, could impose consequences for speeding or make the radio switch from 2Pac to Schumann's Second Symphony
We invest surprisingly little in learning about both sides of ourselves, though failure to understand the gap can bring repeated failures in many aspects of our lives
Many women who are pregnant for the first time tell their doctors before labor that they will refuse painkillers, a decision made when they cannot imagine the pain of childbirth
Modern cars are already full of computers controlling fuel injection, climate, and sound systems, so automatically calling Mom is feasible
Learning how to bridge the hot-cold gap is essential to making some of the important decisions of our lives
It may be that our models of human behavior need rethinking because we may be an agglomeration of multiple selves rather than fully integrated human beings
Perhaps just being aware that we are prone to wrong decisions when gripped by intense emotion may help us apply knowledge of our Hyde selves to daily activities

assets.topic: Discrimination Matrix: The 19-Question Arousal Grid
assets.visual_frame_description: A glowing spreadsheet wall at Sproul Plaza where each question cell splits into cold-blue and hot-red numbers, and the largest percentage gaps flare into pulsing warnings.
assets.player_mission: Sort the appendix's questions into three rows - sexual preferences, immoral behaviors, and birth control - and match each with its cold score, hot score, and percentage difference. Flag the biggest gaps: contact with animals at 167 percent, date-rape persistence at 125 percent, and the drug question at 420 percent, then rate whether each answer would survive the hot state.
key_concepts: Each question was presented on a visual-analog scale stretching from no on the left (zero) to possibly in the middle (50) to yes on the right (100)
Can you imagine being attracted to a 12-year-old girl rose from 23 nonaroused to 46 aroused, a 100 percent difference
Can you imagine having sex with a 60-year-old woman rose from 7 to 23, a 229 percent difference
Could you enjoy having sex with someone you hated rose from 53 to 77, a 45 percent difference
Would you find it exciting to have anal sex rose from 46 to 77, a 67 percent difference
Excitement from contact with an animal rose from 6 to 16, a 167 percent difference
Would you slip a woman a drug to increase the chance that she would have sex with you rose from 5 to 26, a 420 percent difference
Would you tell a woman you loved her to increase the chance of sex rose from 30 to 51, a 70 percent difference
Would you keep trying to have sex after your date says no rose from 20 to 45, a 125 percent difference
Would you always use a condom if you didn't know the sexual history of a new partner fell from 88 nonaroused to 69 aroused, a 22 percent difference
Would you use a condom even if a woman might change her mind while you went to get it fell from 86 to 60, a 30 percent difference
The conclusions were consistent and clear - overwhelmingly clear, frighteningly clear - across all participants and question sets

assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Mr. Hyde Showdown
assets.visual_frame_description: A nightmarish mirror where Dr. Jekyll's calm face is reflected as a sweating, reptilian-eyed Mr. Hyde; between them floats a giant arousal meter and a stack of decision cards marked condom, OnStar, and draft folder.
assets.player_mission: Face the final challenge: predict the size of the hot-cold gap before the reveal, then defend a cold-state decision - condom availability, a speeding car, or an epidural choice - as the arousal meter climbs into the red. Beat Hyde by choosing which real-world safeguard survives the heat of passion.
key_concepts: No matter how we looked at the numbers, the magnitude of underprediction by the participants was substantial
Even the most brilliant and rational person, in the heat of passion, seems to be absolutely and completely divorced from the person he thought he was
When the reptilian brain takes over during arousal, emotions may blur the boundary between what is right and what is wrong
In the heat of passion we are all in danger of switching from 'Just say no' to 'Yes!' in a heartbeat
Widespread availability of condoms is essential because we should not decide in a cool state whether to bring them; they must be there just in case
A better strategy to guarantee teenagers avoid sex is to teach them to walk away from the fire of passion before they are close enough to be drawn in
It is easier to fight temptation before it arises than after it has started to lure us in
Roy is smart, decent, reasonable, and trustworthy most of the time, but unrecognizable to himself when sexually aroused
The study suggested that participants' predictions were not just wrong but wrong by a large margin
He may risk sexually transmitted diseases and unwanted pregnancies in order to achieve sexual gratification
If we don't teach young people how to deal with sex when they are half out of their minds, we are not only fooling them; we're fooling ourselves as well
Sumi's ice bucket test showed that cold-state predictions about pain and childbirth decisions do not match hot-state reality

chapters.title: Chapter 7: The Problem of Procrastination and Self-Control

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: The Deadline Decoder
assets.visual_frame_description: A twelve-week semester timeline stretched across three blackboards, each class drawn as a row of paper deadlines; a red penalty stamp falls one percent per day onto late papers while grade curves settle over the rows.
assets.player_mission: Review the three MIT consumer-behavior classes - self-imposed deadlines, no deadlines, and dictated deadlines - and tag each student's deadline pattern as rational, procrastinating, or precommitted. Spot the students who spaced their papers across the semester and the few who set everything for the last day, then predict the grade ranking of each class.
key_concepts: By 2006 the American personal savings rate had fallen below zero, to negative one percent, with Americans spending more than they earned
Europeans save an average of 20 percent of income, Japan 25 percent, and China 50 percent
The average American family now has six credit cards, and in 2005 alone Americans received 6 billion direct-mail solicitations for credit cards
Average family debt on credit cards is about $9,000, and seven in 10 households borrow on credit cards to cover basic living expenses
Procrastination comes from the Latin pro, meaning for, and cras, meaning tomorrow
In Ariely's consumer behavior class, three papers over the 12-week semester were penalized at one percent off the grade for each day late
A perfectly rational student would set all deadlines for the last day of class, since papers could always be submitted earlier without penalty
Gaurav's class used the scheduling tool to space their deadlines across the whole semester, suggesting students realize their problems with procrastination
The class with dictated deadlines at weeks 4, 8, and 12 got the best grades; the class with no deadlines at all got the worst; the self-deadline class finished in the middle
Simply offering the students a tool by which they could precommit to deadlines helped them achieve better grades
Students who did not space their deadlines sufficiently pulled the class average down with rushed, poorly written final papers
Those who recognize and admit their procrastination weakness are in a better position to utilize precommitment tools to overcome it

assets.topic: Dialogue: The Bank of Self-Control Pitch
assets.visual_frame_description: A plate-glass Manhattan conference room high above rainy yellow cabs, where a mock credit card glows on the table showing limits for coffee, clothing, and chocolate while the executives exchange uneasy glances.
assets.player_mission: Play both sides of the pitch meeting: the enthusiastic professor selling the self-control credit card to half a dozen high-powered bankers overlooking Manhattan, and the bankers weighing $17 billion in yearly interest against a revolutionary product. Negotiate the card's features - category limits, self-selected penalties, cooling-off periods - and decide whether the bank ever calls back.
key_concepts: The self-control credit card would let users decide in advance how much to spend in each category, store, and time frame, such as limiting coffee to $20 every week
Cardholders who surpassed a limit could select their penalties, from having the card rejected to taxing themselves and transferring the tax to Habitat for Humanity
The system could automatically trigger an e-mail to a spouse or friend, such as one noting that Dan Ariely exceeded his $50 monthly chocolate limit by $73.25
The 'ice glass' method puts the credit card in a glass of water in the freezer, so an impulse purchase must wait for the ice to thaw, by which time the compulsion subsides
Tricia, 29, owed $22,302 on her credit cards with a net worth of negative $38,691, and blogged the intimate details of her financial life online
Debt blogging sites such as bloggingawaydebt.com and poorerthanyou.com grew as consumers asked others to help them develop self-control
The bankers were stunned because credit card companies made $17 billion a year in interest from these cards
Ariely argued that one company could step out of the pack by identifying itself as an advocate for the credit-crunched consumer
The executives shook his hand warmly and assured him they would be talking again soon, but they never called him back
The failure may have been due to the $17 billion in interest charges, or maybe it was just good old procrastination
From 1992 to 2004, the rate of debt of Americans age 55 and over rose faster than that of any other group
Smart Cards, thin palm-size cards with impressive computational powers, could be customized to each individual's credit needs

assets.topic: Audit: The Procrastination Prescription Log
assets.visual_frame_description: A clinic waiting room where a wall board like Honda's service menu lists checkup intervals while a freezer holds a credit card in a glass of ice and a $100 refundable deposit form floats toward the nurse's desk.
assets.player_mission: Walk through the chapter's real-world fixes - automatic paycheck deduction, exercise appointments with friends, refundable health-test deposits, and Ford's bundled maintenance intervals - and log the procrastination problem each one solves. For each fix, classify it as dictation, precommitment, or simplification, and rate its expected effect on behavior.
key_concepts: Without precommitments, we keep on falling for temptation and failing to reach our long-term goals
If we can't save from our paycheck, we can take advantage of the employer's automatic deduction option
If we don't have the will to exercise regularly alone, we can make an appointment to exercise in the company of friends
A doctor charging an up-front $100 deposit, refundable only if you show up promptly, would make you more likely to appear for a cholesterol test
For a colonoscopy, a $200 deposit refundable only for arriving on time would replicate the self-imposed deadline condition offered to Gaurav's class
Preventive medicine is generally more cost-effective than the remedial approach, but colonoscopies and mammograms are ordeals people put off
Honda lumped its roughly 18,000 maintenance options into three engineering intervals: every 6 months or 5,000 miles, every year or 10,000 miles, and every two years or 25,000 miles
Ford's service bay was 40 percent vacant until it adopted Honda-style bundling, and in just three years Ford matched Honda's success
The winning argument at Ford was that it is better to have consumers service their vehicles at somewhat compromised intervals than not to service them at all
Bundling medical tests so that people remember to do them is far smarter than adhering to an erratic series of health commands people are unwilling to follow
Thoreau wrote 'Simplify! Simplify!' and simplification is one mark of real genius
Self-imposed deadlines with penalties attached offer a middle ground between authoritarianism and complete freedom to fail

assets.topic: Discrimination Matrix: The Reinforcement Schedule Lab
assets.visual_frame_description: A Skinner box on one side and an inbox on the other: a lever-pressing rat works under a flashing pellet counter while a human thumb scrolls an endless feed; both timelines split into fixed green and variable red reward dots.
assets.player_mission: Sort Skinner's schedules - fixed-ratio versus variable-ratio - and match each to its human counterpart: used-car bonuses, slot machines, e-mail checking, and pellet-pressing rats. Predict which schedule keeps the rat pressing longest after rewards cease, then classify your own e-mail habit and prescribe a fix from the chapter.
key_concepts: Skinner distinguished fixed-ratio schedules, with reward after a fixed number of presses, from variable-ratio schedules with a random number of presses
Under a fixed schedule a rat received food after a fixed number of presses, comparable to a used-car dealer earning $1,000 for every 10 cars sold
Under a variable schedule the rat earned the pellet after a random number of presses, sometimes 10 and sometimes 200
Skinner found variable schedules more motivating: when rewards ceased, fixed-schedule rats stopped almost immediately while variable-schedule rats kept working for a very long time
The variable schedule of reinforcement is the dark magic underlying gambling and the lottery, whose joy comes from unpredictable rewards
E-mail is like gambling: most of it is junk, but the occasional valuable message acts as an unexpected pellet that keeps us pressing the lever
An Australian report found workers spent an average of 14.5 hours a week checking, reading, arranging, deleting, and responding to e-mail
Businesspeople recognize the addictive properties of these devices, which is why they call their BlackBerries 'CrackBerries'
Turning off the automatic e-mail-checking feature reduces the frequency with which the computer notifies us of new mail
Ariely assigns every cc'd e-mail the color gray and sends it to a folder labeled 'Later' to reduce the randomness of the reward
Assigning a cheerful sound to urgent messages made the schedule of reinforcement more fixed and ultimately improved his life
In the movie Seven Pounds, Will Smith's character checks e-mail while driving and veers head-on into a van, killing his wife and six other people

assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Interferon Regimen
assets.visual_frame_description: A loft apartment with a hammock facing a television, a syringe, a refrigerator, and a bucket within reach; a calendar counts down injections as a stack of rental movies grows beside the hammock.
assets.player_mission: Survive the six-month self-control gauntlet: self-inject interferon three times a week and withstand the fever, nausea, and vomiting while everyone else in the protocol skips doses. Deploy your secret weapon - no movies until after the injection - and time the Play button perfectly to beat the side effects and finish the treatment.
key_concepts: Ariely acquired hepatitis from a blood transfusion while hospitalized for burns; in 1993 doctors identified it as hepatitis C
The initial protocol called for self-injections of interferon three times a week for six months, each followed by about 16 hours of fever, nausea, headaches, and vomiting
At the end of the six-month trial, Ariely was the only patient in the protocol who had followed the regimen in the way the doctors designed it
Ariely's trick was to not watch any movies until after injecting himself, then watch as many as he wanted until he fell asleep
Starting the movie immediately after the injection associated the injection with the rewarding experience rather than with the fever and chills
If a desired behavior results in an immediate negative outcome, it will be very difficult to promote even if the ultimate outcome is highly desirable
The second treatment lasted a year and combined interferon with a drug called ribavirin, and it eliminated the hepatitis from his liver
During job interviews he carried his injections in a little icebox and invented excuses to skip dinner so he could inject himself in hotel rooms
The general lesson is to look for tricks that match immediate, powerful, and positive reinforcements with the unpleasant steps toward long-term objectives
Lack of medical compliance is a very pervasive problem
Ralph Keeney estimates that about half of us will make a lifestyle decision that will ultimately lead us to an early grave
Oscar Wilde said, 'I never put off till tomorrow what I can do the day after'

chapters.title: Chapter 8: The High Price of Ownership

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: The Krzyzewskiville Ticket Tell
assets.visual_frame_description: A tent city outside a small stadium under floodlights; each tent glows either seller-red with a $2,400 price or buyer-blue with a $175 offer, and a giant gap splits the two sides of the screen.
assets.player_mission: Call a hundred Duke students the night after the lottery and classify each as ticket owner or non-owner from their price alone. Spot the emotional chasm: buyers anchored near $175 by alternative uses for the money, sellers anchored near $2,400 by memories, and flag the moment when no trade can possibly happen.
key_concepts: Duke students pitch tents in Krzyzewskiville for basketball tickets, with random air-horn occupancy checks that can bump a whole tent to the end of the line
For the most important games, students at the front of the line still did not get a ticket; they received lottery numbers instead
Ariely and Ziv Carmon telephoned ticket winners and non-winners after the lottery in the spring of 1994, becoming ticket scalpers
William, a non-winner, was willing to pay about $175, a price tempered by alternatives like a sports bar, beer, food, CDs, and shoes
Joseph, a winner, demanded about $2,400, justifying the price with the importance of the experience and the lifelong memories it would create
The average selling price of about $2,400 was separated by a factor of about 14 from the average buyer's offer of about $175
Not a single person was willing to sell a ticket at a price that someone else was willing to pay
In an instant after the lottery drawing, students were divided into owners and non-owners, forming an emotional chasm between imagined glory and imagined purchases
From a rational perspective, both groups should have thought of the game in exactly the same way, since enjoyment should not depend on winning a lottery
The predictions were based on the endowment effect research of Jack Knetsch, Dick Thaler, and Daniel Kahneman
The question was whether winners valued tickets more than non-winners even though all the students worked equally hard to obtain them

assets.topic: Dialogue: The Seller's and Buyer's Mirror
assets.visual_frame_description: A driveway split in two: on one side a VW bus glows with golden vacation memories; on the other the buyer squints at a puff of exhaust and a corner of mold while a FOR SALE sign swings overhead.
assets.player_mission: Play both sides of a VW bus sale and a house sale: the seller reliving mountain trips and sunlight-filtering kitchen windows, and the buyer noticing the puff of smoke shifting from first to second gear and the black mold in the corner. Run both negotiations and decide when each perspective mismatch leads to an inflated price or a lost sale.
key_concepts: The first quirk of ownership is that we fall in love with what we already have, recalling warm trips and memories even before the FOR SALE sign goes up
The Chinese adoption story: the director randomly presented each of 12 couples a daughter, yet all felt the matches were perfect
What made each match seem perfect was not the director's talent but nature's ability to make us instantly attached to what we have
The second quirk is that we focus on what we may lose rather than what we may gain when pricing a possession
Our aversion to loss is a strong emotion that sometimes causes us to make bad decisions
As soon as we begin thinking about giving up our valued possessions, we are already mourning the loss
The third quirk is that we assume other people will see the transaction from the same perspective as we do
The buyer of the VW is more likely to notice the puff of smoke when you shift from first into second than your memories
The buyer of your house is more likely to notice the strip of black mold in the corner than the sunlight through the kitchen windows
The friend who sold a whole box of records for $25 at a garage sale saw the buyer sell them for ten times that the next day
If we always overvalued what we had, there would be no such thing as Antiques Roadshow
Ownership also applies to points of view, and once we prize an idea too much we are left with a rigid, unyielding ideology

assets.topic: Audit: The Ownership Audit Trail
assets.visual_frame_description: A cluttered living room where each trap appears as a glowing exhibit: an auction countdown, a cable bill marked digital gold, a sofa with a money-back tag, and a blueprint of a wall being torn down and later rebuilt.
assets.player_mission: Audit five ownership traps from the chapter - the online auction spiral, the digital gold trial package, the 30-day money-back sofa, the remodeled Cambridge house, and the VW sale - and log how each one triggers the three irrational quirks. Note the moment virtual ownership took over in each and the price ultimately paid.
key_concepts: The more work you put into something, the more ownership you begin to feel for it, a phenomenon Mike Norton and Ariely call the 'Ikea effect'
Pride of ownership is inversely proportional to the ease with which one assembles the furniture
In online auctions, the participant who is the highest bidder for the longest period ends up with the strongest feelings of virtual ownership
James Heyman, Yesim Orhun, and Ariely found that once bidders thought of themselves as owners, they were compelled to bid higher and higher to prevent losing their position
Virtual ownership is one mainspring of the advertising industry, from BMW convertibles to Patagonia fleece
Cable trial promotions like digital gold at $59 instead of $89 hook customers because once we have the package, downgrading becomes a loss we cannot bear
The 30-day money-back guarantee pushes us to take the sofa home, where returning it starts to feel like a loss
In the second quarter of 2008, 92 percent of home owners said there had been foreclosures in their local real estate market and were concerned about home values
Two out of three home owners (62 percent) believed the value of their own home had increased or stayed the same while the market collapsed
Ariely and Sumi tore down walls for an open feel in their Cambridge house and converted the carriage house, yet no buyer made an offer
Their real estate agent said they would have to rebuild some walls and reverse their changes; a few weeks after they did, the house was sold
In the end, the buyers didn't want their home; they wanted theirs, an expensive lesson in overvaluing our modifications

assets.topic: Discrimination Matrix: The Value Gap Grid
assets.visual_frame_description: A wall of glowing price tags in a stadium concourse, each buyer-seller pair separated by a red chasm while a factor-of-14 ruler hovers above the basketball ticket pair.
assets.player_mission: Sort every price in the chapter into buyer values and seller values - $175 versus $2,400 tickets, the garage-sale album box, Zillow's home values, and the Cambridge house - and compute each gap. Flag the emotional driver on each side, from memories to sports bars, and mark which gaps rational analysis simply cannot close.
key_concepts: William's buyer price of $175 was tempered by what the money could alternatively buy: the sports bar, beer and food, CDs, or shoes
Joseph's seller price of $2,400 rested on the game being a defining memory of his time at Duke, an experience to pass on to his children and grandchildren
The average selling price of about $2,400 exceeded the average buyer's offer of about $175 by a factor of about 14
The positivity bias, called the Lake Wobegon Effect, holds that all the women are strong, all the men are good-looking, and all the children are above average
We feel we are better-than-average drivers, more likely to be able to afford retirement, and less likely to get a parking ticket for overstaying a meter
Zillow found that two out of three home owners believed the value of their own home had increased or stayed the same as the housing market collapsed
About half of home owners (56 percent) planned to invest in home improvements even as they watched the housing market collapse
After each set of prospective buyers left the Cambridge house, the couple said to each other that the people were dull and unimaginative and had no taste
The house sold only after a contractor re-erected walls, an expensive lesson about the effect of modifications on potential buyers
From a rational perspective, the anticipated atmosphere at the game and its enjoyment should not depend on winning a lottery
There is no known cure for the ills of ownership, which Adam Smith said is woven into our lives
Downgrading to a smaller home is experienced as a loss that is psychologically painful, even if the monthly mortgage sinks our ship

assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Endowment Gauntlet
assets.visual_frame_description: A courtroom of ownership where your childhood house, your VW bus, and your cherished opinion sit on the witness stand; each quirk rises as a gavel-smashing hologram while a Zillow-style market line crashes behind the judge.
assets.player_mission: Defend the final asset - your cherished opinion - against the three ownership quirks: the love of what you have, the fear of loss, and the assumption that others see it your way. Price your possession as a nonowner, accept the agent's verdict on your rebuilt walls, and break the Lake Wobegon spell before the market collapses around you.
key_concepts: Ownership fundamentally changes our perspective, and suddenly moving backward to our pre-ownership state is a loss we cannot abide
Once we take ownership of an idea, we love it perhaps more than we should, prize it more than it is worth, and have trouble letting go
We overvalue everything that we own, whether basketball tickets or domiciles, the same way we think our own kids are more wonderful than our friends' children
Home ownership is more complex than a coffee mug because we invest so much in our houses, from granite countertops to koi ponds
The owner of the beautifully remodeled house understands why the other homes languished on the market: 'they simply are not as nice as mine'
The Cambridge house cost double mortgages, double heating bills, and double taxes while the housing market continued to slow down
Being aware of ownership biases might help us listen more carefully to the advice and feedback we get from others
The Lake Wobegon Effect reflects a more general tendency to fall in love with, and be overly optimistic about, anything that has to do with ourselves
We may not become more accurate and objective about our children and houses, but we can realize that we have such biases
The buyers didn't want the remodeled home; they wanted theirs, no matter how convinced the sellers were of their superior taste
We are willing to make all kinds of sacrifices to avoid the psychologically painful loss of downgrading
Ariely tries to view all transactions, particularly large ones, as if he were a nonowner, attempting to be as Zen as he can about material things

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: The Door-Game Dilemma
assets.visual_frame_description: A dark MIT East Campus hallway where a laptop screen shows three doors shrinking as Sam's cursor darts between them; beside him a scoreboard compares his frantic clicks with Albert's calm, profitable strategy.
assets.player_mission: Watch Sam race through the disappearing-doors version of the game and tag each of his clicks as exploration, exploitation, or panic-rescue. Count the clicks wasted on keeping doors alive, then compare his earnings with Albert's, who sampled every room, returned to the best one, and stayed there.
key_concepts: In 210 BC, Xiang Yu burned his ships and crushed his cooking pots after crossing the Yangtze, leaving his troops no choice but to fight, and they won nine consecutive battles
Xiang Yu's story is completely antithetical to normal human behavior, since normally we cannot stand the idea of closing the doors on our alternatives
We buy expandable computer systems, TV insurance policies, and luxury SUVs just in case, giving up time and money for worthless options
In the door game, three colored doors led to rooms that paid between one cent and 10 cents per click, with a total of 100 clicks available
Each move from one room to another cost one click, so running from door to door burned up earnings
Albert sampled all three rooms, went back to the best one, and spent the remainder of his 100 clicks there, earning one of the best scores so far
In the disappearing condition, any door left unvisited for 12 clicks would disappear forever
Sam frenziedly raced from door to door, clicking each one to restore it to full size before it vanished
Participants in the frenzy to keep doors from shutting made substantially less money, about 15 percent less, than those who didn't have to deal with closing doors
They could have made more money by picking a room, any room, and merely staying there for the whole experiment
Charging three cents per door opening, revealing exact monetary outcomes, and allowing hundreds of practice trials all failed to change the behavior
Even a door that could be brought back to life with a single click was still defended, because participants couldn't tolerate the idea of the loss

assets.topic: Dialogue: The Two-Major Crossroads
assets.visual_frame_description: A cavernous MIT atrium split into two mirrored lecture halls - one filled with drafting tables and blueprints, the other with server racks - while two students stand at the intersection holding course lists that refuse to overlap.
assets.player_mission: Counsel Joe at the MIT crossroads between architecture and computer science, then counsel Dana between two boyfriends, playing both voices in each conversation. Push them to name what they lose by keeping both doors open, and decide which door each should close before the semester swallows them.
key_concepts: Joe, an incoming junior, had a passion for architecture and a liking for computer science, and the required courses for the two majors were incompatible
If Joe signed up for classes in both disciplines, he would most likely end up without a degree in either field and would need another year, paid for by his parents
Joe eventually graduated with a degree in computer science and found the perfect blend in his first job designing nuclear subs for the Navy
Dana could not let go of a previous relationship that was dying while her new boyfriend grew restless
Ariely asked Dana if she would risk losing the boy she loved for the remote possibility that she might love her former boyfriend more
We give up the chance that our children could become really good at one activity by spreading them across gymnastics, piano, French, and tae kwon do
In running back and forth among the things that might be important, we forget to spend enough time on what really is important
Erich Fromm's 1941 book Escape from Freedom described people beset not by a lack of opportunity but by a dizzying abundance of it
We must develop ourselves in every way possible and taste every aspect of life, spreading ourselves too thin
We chase after doors of little worth, like nourishing a wilting relationship or buying on sale just because the price will never come again
Some doors close too slowly for us to see them vanishing, such as the childhood of our sons and daughters slipping away while we work
A friend's single best year of marriage came when he and his wife lived apart and met only on weekends, making their shared time limited with a clear end

assets.topic: Audit: The Open-Door Cost Ledger
assets.visual_frame_description: A cluttered family garage where each possession sprouts a glowing price tag of hidden costs - insurance, upgrades, lessons, tuition - while a ledger column labeled cost of keeping open grows taller than the door.
assets.player_mission: Audit every open door in the chapter - the expandable computer, the TV warranty, the SUV clearance, Joe's double major, Dana's two boyfriends, and the sale-shopping habit - and bill each one its true cost in clicks, time, money, and attention. Close the doors whose upkeep exceeds their option value.
key_concepts: We end up with a computer that has more functions than we need and a stereo with an unnecessarily expensive warranty
Keeping children in every activity gives up their time and ours, and the chance that they could become really good at one activity
We buy things on sale not because we really need them but because once the sale ends we could never have them at that price again
Ariely's own MIT versus Stanford decision consumed weeks of comparing schools, neighborhoods, and jobs while his research productivity began to suffer
Ironically, as he searched for the best place to do his work, his research was being neglected
Congress frequently gridlocks itself over the details of legislation, stuck in the middle like the donkey between two haystacks
A friend spent three months selecting a digital camera from two nearly identical models, missing months of family photo opportunities
The donkey in the story stood between two haystacks of identical size and eventually died of starvation because it couldn't decide
The donkey, Congress, and the friend all failed to take into account the consequences of not deciding
They also failed to consider the relatively minor differences that would have come with either one of the decisions
The friend would have been equally happy with either camera, and the donkey could have eaten either bale of hay
They should have considered the decision an easy one and gotten on with their lives, but we don't act that way because we can't close those doors

assets.topic: Discrimination Matrix: The Option-Value Grid
assets.visual_frame_description: A two-axis scatter plot floating above a game screen, with doors plotted by payoff and upkeep cost; the keep-open zone shrinks as loss-aversion red spreads across the grid.
assets.player_mission: Rate every door in the game and in life on two axes - true payoff versus cost of keeping open - and sort them into keep, close, and never-open columns. Score the disappearing-door runs, the three-cent door tax, the revealed-payout condition, and the reincarnating door, and decide which fixation is pure loss aversion.
key_concepts: When each click opening a door cost three cents, participants showed no difference in response and still had the same irrational excitement about keeping options open
When told the exact monetary outcomes they could expect from each room, participants still could not stand to see a door close
Even with hundreds of practice trials, MIT students could not stay focused once they saw their options shrinking
In the reincarnating condition, a single click could bring a vanished door back to life, yet participants still wasted clicks on it
The reincarnating door's disappearance had no real consequences and could always be easily reversed, but the loss was still intolerable
Pecking like barnyard hens at every door, participants sought to make more money and ended up making far less
Running from pillar to post was not only stressful but uneconomical
Jiwoong Shin of Yale and Ariely devised the door game to capture the dilemma represented by Joe and Dana
The experiment location was MIT's East Campus dormitory, home to hackers, hardware enthusiasts, oddballs, and general misfits
Getting the most money out of the experiment involved finding the room with the biggest payoff and clicking in it as many times as possible
Switching from one room to another could be a good strategy for finding the biggest payout, but it burned clicks that could have made money
The frenzy to keep doors from closing cost participants about 15 percent less in earnings than those with no closing doors

assets.topic: Boss Battle: The Closing-Door Finale
assets.visual_frame_description: A plantation staircase at dusk where Scarlett begs 'Where shall I go?' and Rhett turns away; behind him a row of doors - committee, golf, ex, Stanford - slam one by one while a single door glows at the end of a hallway.
assets.player_mission: Stand where Rhett Butler stood and close your doors deliberately: drop the committee, cut the sport, end the stale relationship, and make the MIT-or-Stanford call. Survive the two-option paralysis of donkey, Congress, and camera alike, and walk away with one door open, chosen, and committed.
key_concepts: Rhett Butler's 'Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn' was voted the most memorable line in cinematographic history, and its appeal comes from the emphatic closing of a door
What we need is to consciously start closing some of our doors, and small doors are rather easy to close, like striking names off holiday card lists
Bigger doors tied to new careers, better jobs, dreams, and relationships are harder to close even when they seem to be going nowhere
We ought to shut doors because they draw energy and commitment away from the doors that should be left open, and because they drive us crazy
